{{Short description|none}}

[[File:Flag on Saddam Firdos Square Statues face 2003-04-09.jpg|thumb|[[United States Marine Corps|U.S. Marines]] raise the [[U.S. flag]] over [[Saddam Hussein statue destruction|Saddam Hussein's statue]] during the 2003 [[Iraq War]].]]
[[File:LC-DIG-GGBAIN-15834 (17523460795).jpg|thumb|U.S. Marines raise the U.S. flag over [[Battle of Veracruz (1914)|Veracruz, Mexico]] during the [[Banana Wars]].]]
{{AmericanEmpire}}
The United States has been involved in hundreds of interventions in foreign countries throughout [[History of the United States|its history]], engaging in nearly 500 military interventions between 1776 and 2026, with half of these operations occurring since 1950 and over 25% occurring in the post-[[Cold War]] period.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Kushi |first1=Sidita |last2=Toft |first2=Monica Duffy |title=Introducing the Military Intervention Project: A New Dataset on US Military Interventions, 1776–2019 |journal=Journal of Conflict Resolution |date=2023 |volume=67 |issue=4 |pages=752–779 |doi=10.1177/00220027221117546 }}</ref> Common objectives of U.S. foreign interventions have historically revolved around economic opportunity, protection of U.S. citizens and diplomats, [[American imperialism|territorial expansion]], [[counterterrorism]], fomenting [[United States involvement in regime change|regime change]] and [[nation-building]], [[Democracy promotion by the United States|promoting democracy]], providing [[United States foreign aid|aid]] and enforcing [[international law]].<ref name=":0" /> There have been two dominant ideologies in the United States regarding foreign policy—[[Interventionism (politics)|interventionism]], which encourages military and political intervention in the affairs of foreign countries—and [[United States non-interventionism|isolationism]], which discourages these.<ref>Wertheim, "Tomorrow The World," 2020, p4.</ref>

The 19th century formed the roots of United States foreign interventionism, which at the time was largely driven by economic opportunities in the Pacific and Spanish-held Latin America along with the [[Monroe Doctrine]], which saw the U.S. seek a policy to resist [[History of colonialism|European colonialism]] in the [[Western Hemisphere]]. The 20th century saw the U.S. intervene in two [[world war]]s in which American forces fought alongside their allies in international campaigns against [[Empire of Japan|Imperial Japan]], [[German Empire|Imperial]] and [[Nazi Germany]], and their respective allies. The [[aftermath of World War II]] resulted in a foreign policy of [[containment]] aimed at preventing the spread of [[world communism]]. The ensuing [[Cold War]] resulted in the [[Truman Doctrine|Truman]], [[Eisenhower Doctrine|Eisenhower]], [[Kennedy Doctrine|Kennedy]], [[Carter Doctrine|Carter]], and [[Reagan Doctrine]]s, all of which saw the U.S. engage in [[Cold War espionage|espionage]], [[regime change]], [[proxy war]]s, and other [[Clandestine operation|clandestine activity]] internationally against affiliates and puppet regimes of the [[Soviet Union]]. The [[Nixon Doctrine]] reaffirmed the [[nuclear umbrella]] but wanted U.S. allies to be self-dependent, as exemplified by [[Vietnamization]].

After the Soviet Union [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|collapsed]] in 1991, the U.S. emerged as the world's sole [[superpower]] and, with this, maintained interventionist policies in Africa, Eastern Europe, and the Middle East. Following the [[September 11 attacks]] in 2001, the [[Presidency of George W. Bush|Bush administration]] launched the "[[war on terror]]" in which the U.S. waged international [[counterterrorism]] campaigns against various extremist groups—such as [[al-Qaeda]] and the [[Islamic State]]—in various countries. The [[Bush Doctrine]] of [[preemptive war]] saw the U.S. [[United States invasion of Afghanistan|invade Afghanistan]] in 2001 and [[2003 invasion of Iraq|Iraq]] in 2003. In addition, the U.S. expanded its military presence in Africa and Asia via [[status of forces agreement]]s and a revamped policy of [[foreign internal defense]].

The [[Presidency of Barack Obama|Obama administration]]'s 2012 [[East Asian foreign policy of the Barack Obama administration|Pivot to Asia]] strategy sought to refocus U.S. geopolitical efforts from counter-insurgencies in the Middle East to improving American diplomatic influence and military presence in [[East Asia]], reinforcing the [[Island chain strategy|first island chain]] and countering China's rising influence and perceived expansionism in the [[South China Sea]] —a trajectory continued by the [[Foreign policy of the first Donald Trump administration|Trump]] (2017–2021, 2025–present) and [[Foreign policy of the Joe Biden administration|Biden]] administrations under the [[Free and Open Indo-Pacific]] (FOIP) strategy. The [[Foreign policy of the second Trump administration|second Trump administration]] introduced the [[Monroe Doctrine#America First and Trump Corollary: The "Donroe Doctrine"|Trump Corollary]] to the Monroe Doctrine, aiming to consolidate US dominance in the Western Hemisphere and prevent Chinese, Russian and other adversarial powers from meddling in "[[America's Backyard|America's backyard]]." In January 2026, the US [[2026 United States intervention in Venezuela|intervened]] in [[Venezuela]], capturing President [[Nicolas Maduro]] and constraining his government. The next month, the United States and [[Israel]] jointly attacked [[Iran]], killing Iranian supreme leader [[Ali Khamenei]] and [[List of Iranian officials killed during the 2026 Iran war|other Iranian leaders]], sparking the ongoing [[2026 Iran war]].

The [[United States Navy]] serves as a key element of United States global [[power projection]] and its ability to conduct foreign interventions. As a [[blue-water navy]], it has been involved in anti-[[piracy]] activity in [[International waters|international]] and foreign territory throughout its history, from the [[Barbary Wars]] to [[United States Naval Forces Central Command|combating]] modern [[piracy off the coast of Somalia]] and other regions. The [[United States Air Force]]'s strategic [[airlift]] and [[Strategic bombing|global strike]] capabilities alongside clandestine activity by [[United States special operations forces|special operations units]] are two other major components in US [[hard power]] projection.

== Post-colonial ==
{{Main|History of U.S. foreign policy, 1776–1801|History of U.S. foreign policy, 1801–1829|History of U.S. foreign policy, 1829–1861|History of U.S. foreign policy, 1861–1897}}
{{See also|Territorial evolution of the United States|America's Backyard}}
[[File:Battle of Nassau.jpg|thumb|American [[Thirteen Colonies|colonial]] forces [[Raid of Nassau|raided Nassau]] during the [[American Revolutionary War|Revolutionary War]] in March 1776, as depicted by an artist in 1973.]]
[[File:Attack on Derna by Charles Waterhouse 01.jpg|thumb|The 1805 [[Battle of Derna (1805)|Battle of Derna]], the first foreign United States military victory, as depicted by [[Charles Waterhouse (artist)|Charles Waterhouse]].]]
[[File:Sujagi.jpg|thumb|[[United States Marine Corps|Marines]] of the [[Asiatic Squadron]] with the captured ''[[Sujagi]]'' during the 1871 [[United States expedition to Korea|Korean Expedition]]. The flag was returned to Korea in 2007.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.shinmiyangyo.org/old/baltimoresun.html|title=Korean flag to be returned on loan basis|accessdate=27 January 2015|publisher=Baltimore Sun|author=Bradley Olson|date=11 October 2007}}</ref>]]
[[File:TR San Juan Hill 1898.jpg|thumb|Colonel [[Theodore Roosevelt]] and the [[Rough Riders]] after [[Battle of San Juan Hill|capturing]] [[San Juan Hill]] during the [[Spanish–American War]]]]

The 18th-19th century saw the United States transition from an [[United States non-interventionism|isolationist]], post-[[Thirteen Colonies|colonial]] regional power to a Trans-Atlantic and Trans-Pacific [[maritime power]]. From 1790 to 1797, the [[United States Revenue Cutter Service|U.S. Revenue Marine]] served as the United States' only armed maritime service, tasked with enforcing [[Customs|export duties]], and was the predecessor to the [[United States Coast Guard]]. The [[Naval Act of 1794|1794 Naval Act]] authorized the construction of the [[Original six frigates of the United States Navy|first six frigates]] of what would subsequently become the permanent [[United States Navy]]. Throughout the century, the United States increasingly engaged in [[gunboat diplomacy]] to intimidate less powerful entities and fulfill foreign policy objectives. President [[James K. Polk]] was an advocate of American expansionism under [[Manifest Destiny]] and saw U.S. territory reach the [[Pacific Ocean]], setting the foundations for future U.S. power projection and interventionism. 

The [[First Barbary War|first]] and [[second Barbary War]]s of the early 19th century were the first nominal foreign wars waged by the United States following independence. Directed against the [[Barbary States]] of North Africa, the [[Barbary Wars]] were fought to end piracy against American-flagged ships in the Mediterranean Sea, similar to the [[Undeclared war|undeclared]] "[[Quasi-War]]" with the [[French First Republic|French Republic]] from 1798 to 1800.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.globalsecurity.org/military/ops/barbary.htm|title=Barbary Wars|author=John Pike|work=globalsecurity.org}}</ref> The founding of [[Liberia]] was privately sponsored by American groups, primarily the [[American Colonization Society]], but the country enjoyed the support and unofficial cooperation of the United States government.<ref>Flint, John E. ''The Cambridge History of Africa: from c.1790 to c.1870'' Cambridge University Press (1976) pg 184-199</ref> 

Notable 19th century interventions included:
* 1803–1860: The United States [[Louisiana Purchase|purchases]] the [[Louisiana (New France)|Louisiana territory]] from [[French First Republic|France]] in 1803, expanding its sovereignty west of the [[Mississippi River]] and nearly doubling the nominal size of the country across North America. The [[treaty of 1818]] establishes a boundary along the [[49th parallel north]] between [[Rupert's Land]] and the U.S. In 1853, the U.S. [[Gadsden Purchase|purchases]] 29,640-square-mile (76,800 km2) of land from [[Second Federal Republic of Mexico|Mexico]], defining the [[Mexico–United States border]].
* 1811: U.S. federal agent [[Joel Roberts Poinsett]] arrives in [[Chile]] to assess the prospects of Chilean revolutionaries during their [[Chilean War of Independence|war]] against the [[Spanish Empire]], leading the first of [[United States intervention in Chile|many U.S. interventions]] in Chile.
* 1846–1848: During the [[Mexican–American War]], Mexico and the United States warred over [[Texas Campaign|Texas]], [[Conquest of California|California]], and what today is the [[American Southwest]] but was then part of [[Second Federal Republic of Mexico|Mexico]]. During this war, [[United States Armed Forces|U.S. Armed Forces]] troops invaded and occupied parts of Mexico, including [[Siege of Veracruz|Veracruz]] and [[Battle for Mexico City|Mexico City]].
* 1854: Commodore [[Matthew C. Perry]] negotiated the [[Convention of Kanagawa]], which effectively ended Japan's centuries of [[Sakoku|national isolation]], opening the country to [[Western world|Western]] trade and diplomacy.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.history.navy.mil/branches/teach/ends/opening.htm |title=Perry & Opening of Japan |access-date=2011-08-04 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110805041252/http://www.history.navy.mil/branches/teach/ends/opening.htm |archive-date=2011-08-05 }}</ref> From 1863 to 1864, U.S. forces participated in the [[Shimonoseki campaign]], a conflict over Japan's open-door policy as a result of Perry's expedition.
* 1854–1949: The [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]] launches the [[Yangtze Patrol]] in 1854, an operation to protect U.S. interests, merchant ships and citizens in [[Qing dynasty|China]]'s [[Yangtze]] river [[treaty ports]] and along China's coast. The mission was permanently ended in 1949 amid the [[Chinese Civil War]]. 
* 1858–1859: President [[James Buchanan]] dispatched a diplomatic mission and [[Paraguay expedition|nineteen-ship squadron]] to Paraguay under the auspices of seeking reparations for previous Paraguayan aggression against U.S. citizens.
* 1871: The U.S. dispatched an [[United States expedition to Korea|expeditionary force]] to [[Joseon|Korea]] after failed attempts to ascertain the fate of the armed merchant ship [[General Sherman incident|''General Sherman'']], which was attacked during an unsuccessful attempt to [[Western imperialism in Asia|open up trade]] with the isolationist kingdom in 1866. After being [[Bombardment of the Selee River Forts|ambushed]], the 650-man American expeditionary force launched a [[Punitive expedition|punitive campaign]], capturing and occupying several Korean forts and killing over 200 Korean troops.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Roblin|first=Sebastien|date=2018-01-18|title=In 1871, America 'Invaded' Korea. Here's What Happened.|url=https://nationalinterest.org/blog/the-buzz/1871-america-invaded-korea-heres-what-happened-24113|access-date=2021-04-14|website=The National Interest|language=en}}</ref>
* 1887–1889: U.S. and [[Imperial German Navy|German naval forces]] engaged in a months-long [[Samoan crisis|standoff]] over control of the [[Samoan Islands]] during the [[Samoan Civil War]]. The standoff ended when a [[1889 Apia cyclone|cyclone]] wrecked all six ships involved. The 1899 [[Tripartite Convention]] partitioned the islands into [[American Samoa]] and [[German Samoa]].
* 1898: The short but decisive [[Spanish–American War]] saw overwhelming American victories at sea and on land against the Spanish Kingdom. The U.S. Army, relying significantly on volunteers and state militia units, invaded and occupied [[Spanish Cuba|Spanish-controlled Cuba]], subsequently granting it independence. The [[Treaty of Paris (1898)|peace treaty]] saw Spain cede control over its colonies of [[Spanish Puerto Rico|Puerto Rico]], [[Guam]], and the [[History of the Philippines (1565–1898)|Philippines]] to the United States.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.digitalhistory.uh.edu/database/article_display.cfm?HHID=191 |title=The Philippines |date=22 May 2011 |work=Digital History |publisher=[[University of Houston]] |access-date=22 May 2011 |quote=In December, Spain ceded the Philippines to the United States for $20 million. |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111025024629/http://www.digitalhistory.uh.edu/database/article_display.cfm?HHID=191 |archive-date=25 October 2011 |df=dmy-all }}</ref> The U.S. Navy set up [[Fuelling station|coaling stations]] there and in [[Territory of Hawaii|Hawaii]].<ref>William Braisted, ''United States Navy in the Pacific, 1897–1909'' (2008)</ref> See also: [[Bath Iron Works]]
* 1899: The U.S. advanced the [[Open Door Policy]] to guarantee equal economic access to [[Qing dynasty|China]] and support of Chinese territorial and administrative integrity.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/429642/Open-Door-policy|title=Open Door policy|encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica}}</ref>

[[File:Siege of Peking, Boxer Rebellion.jpg|thumb|U.S. [[14th Infantry Regiment (United States)|14th Infantry Regiment]] assaulting [[Beijing city fortifications|Peking]] during the [[Boxer Rebellion]]]]
[[File:BigStickinLAmerica.jpg|thumb|right|A map of [[Middle America (Americas)|Middle America]] showing the places affected by [[Theodore Roosevelt]]'s [[Big stick policy]]]]
The early decades of the 20th century saw a number of interventions in Latin America by the U.S. government often justified under the [[Roosevelt Corollary]] to the [[Monroe Doctrine]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theodoreroosevelt.org/life/rooseveltcorollary.htm|title=Home - Theodore Roosevelt Association|work=theodoreroosevelt.org}}</ref> President [[William Howard Taft]] viewed [[Dollar diplomacy]] as a way for American corporations to benefit while assisting in the [[national security]] goal of preventing European powers from filling any possible financial power vacuum.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.americanforeignrelations.com/A-D/Dollar-Diplomacy.html|title=Dollar Diplomacy|work=americanforeignrelations.com}}</ref> The ''[[Small Wars Manual]]'' outlined the role [[United States Marine Corps|U.S. Marines]] served as an [[Expeditionary warfare|expeditionary force]] to project power and police countries in the U.S.'s sphere of influence. Marines were often deployed to safeguard customs revenues which were the cause of local civil wars.<ref>Lester D. Langley, ''The Banana Wars: United States Intervention in the Caribbean, 1898–1934'' (2001)</ref>
* 1898–1935: The U.S. launched multiple minor interventions ([[Banana Wars]]) into Latin America, resulting in U.S. military presence in [[United States Military Government in Cuba|Cuba]], [[History of Honduras#The internationalization of the north, 1899–1932|Honduras]], [[Panama Canal Zone|Panama]] (via the [[Hay–Bunau-Varilla Treaty]] and [[Isthmian Canal Commission]]),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/panama-declares-independence|title=Panama declares independence|work=HISTORY.com|date=March 4, 2010 }}</ref> [[United States occupation of Haiti|Haiti]] (1915–1935),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://2001-2009.state.gov/r/pa/ho/time/wwi/88275.htm|title=U.S. Invasion and Occupation of Haiti, 1915-34|first=Bureau of Public Affairs|last=Department Of State. The Office of Electronic Information|date=July 13, 2007|website=2001-2009.state.gov}}</ref> the [[United States occupation of the Dominican Republic (1916–1924)|Dominican Republic]] (1916–1924), and [[United States occupation of Nicaragua|Nicaragua]] (1912–1925; 1926–1933).<ref>{{cite news| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/1225283.stm | work=BBC News | title=Nicaragua timeline | date=9 November 2011}}</ref>
** 1901: The [[Platt Amendment]] amended a treaty between the U.S. and the [[Republic of Cuba (1902–1959)|Republic of Cuba]] after the Spanish–American War, virtually making Cuba a U.S. protectorate. The amendment outlined conditions for the U.S. to intervene in Cuban affairs and permitted the United States to lease or buy lands for the purpose of the establishing naval bases, including [[Guantanamo Bay Naval Base|Guantánamo Bay]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ourdocuments.gov/doc.php?flash=true&doc=55|title=Our Documents - Platt Amendment (1903)|work=ourdocuments.gov|date=April 9, 2021 }}</ref>
** 1904: When European governments began to use force to pressure Latin American countries to repay their debts, [[Theodore Roosevelt]] announced his "[[Roosevelt Corollary|Corollary]]" to the Monroe Doctrine, stating that the United States would not just prevent but militarily intervene in affairs between European and Latin American governments if European pressure resulted in the Latin countries becoming chronically unstable [[failed states]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ourdocuments.gov/doc.php?flash=true&doc=56|title=Our Documents - Theodore Roosevelt's Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (1905)|work=ourdocuments.gov|date=April 9, 2021 }}</ref>
** 1906–1909: The U.S. governed Cuba under Governor [[Charles Magoon]].<ref>{{cite journal|jstor=3739793|title=Agriculture in Cuba during the Second United States Intervention, 1906-1909|first=David A.|last=Lockmiller|date=1 January 1937|journal=Agricultural History|volume=11|issue=3|pages=181–188}}</ref>
** 1914: During a revolution in the Dominican Republic, the U.S. Navy fired at revolutionaries who were bombarding [[Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic|Puerto Plata]], in order to stop the action.
** 1916 to 1924: [[United States occupation of the Dominican Republic (1916–1924)|U.S. Marines occupied the Dominican Republic]] following 28 revolutions in 50 years.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://millercenter.org/president/keyevents/roosevelt|title=Presidential Key Events|work=millercenter.org|access-date=August 4, 2011|archive-date=August 11, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110811225744/http://millercenter.org/president/keyevents/roosevelt|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Marines ruled the nation completely except for lawless parts of the city of [[Santo Domingo]], where warlords still held sway.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thoughtco.com/us-occupation-of-the-dominican-republic-2136380|title=Why Did the USA Occupy the Dominican Republic in 1916?|first1=Spanish|last1=Ph. D.|first2=Spanish|last2=M. A.|first3=Spanish|last3=B. A.|website=ThoughtCo}}</ref>
* 1899–1901: The U.S. organized the [[China Relief Expedition]] during the [[Boxer Rebellion]], which saw an eight-nation alliance put down a rebellion by the [[Boxer movement|Boxer]] secret society and toppled the [[Qing dynasty]]'s Imperial Army.
* 1899–1913: The [[Philippine–American War]] saw [[First Philippine Republic|Filipino revolutionaries]] revolt against [[Treaty of Paris (1898)|American annexation]] following the Spanish-American War. The U.S. Army deployed 100,000 (mostly [[National Guard (United States)|National Guard]]) troops under General [[Elwell Otis]] to the Philippines, resulting in the poorly armed and poorly trained rebels to break off into armed bands. The insurgency collapsed in March 1901 when the leader, [[Emilio Aguinaldo]], was captured by General [[Frederick Funston]] and his [[Philippine Scouts|Macabebe]] allies.<ref>[[Brian McAllister Linn]], ''The Philippine War 1899–1902'' (University Press of Kansas, 2000). {{ISBN|0-7006-0990-3}}</ref> The concurrent [[Moro Rebellion]] concluded at the [[Battle of Bud Bagsak]] in June 1913.
* 1910–1919: The [[Mexican Border War]] along the [[U.S.-Mexico border]] saw U.S. forces [[United States occupation of Veracruz|occupy]] [[Veracruz]] for six months in 1914. U.S. troops intervened in northern Mexico during the [[Pancho Villa Expedition]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.veteranmuseum.org/us-mexico.html|title=United States Interventions in Mexico, 1914-1917|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040327212349/http://www.veteranmuseum.org/us-mexico.html|archive-date=March 27, 2004 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 1917–1920: The U.S. [[United States in World War I|intervened in Europe]] during [[World War I]]. Over the next 18 months, the U.S. would suffer casualties of 116,708 killed and 204,002 wounded. U.S. troops also [[Allied intervention in the Russian Civil War|intervened]] in the [[Russian Civil War]] against the [[Red Army]] via the [[Siberian intervention]] and the [[Polar Bear Expedition]]'s [[North Russia intervention]].

=== World War II ===
{{Main|Military history of the United States during World War II|List of World War II battles involving the United States}}

[[File:Ronson flame tank Iwo Jima.jpg|thumb|U.S. [[M4 Sherman]] tank clearing an [[Empire of Japan|Imperial Japanese]] bunker on [[Battle of Iwo Jima|Iwo Jima]] during the [[Second World War]]]]

A [[Neutrality Acts of the 1930s|series of Neutrality Acts]] passed by the [[United States Congress|U.S. Congress]] in the 1930s sought to return foreign policy to non-interventionism in European affairs, as it had been prior to the [[American entry into World War I]]. However, [[Nazi Germany]]'s [[U-boat]] attacks on American vessels in 1941 saw many provisions of the Neutrality Acts largely revoked. The [[Two-Ocean Navy Act]] of 1940 would ultimately increase the size of the United States Navy by 70%.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hutcheson|first=John A. Jr. |title=Encyclopedia of World War II: A Political, Social, and Military History|page=1541}}</ref> The British-American [[destroyers-for-bases deal]] in September 1940 saw the U.S. transfer 50 Navy destroyers to the [[Royal Navy]] in exchange for rent-free, [[99-year lease]]s over various British imperial possessions. The U.S. gained the land rights to establish new military bases in [[Antigua]], [[British Guiana]], [[Dominion of Newfoundland|Newfoundland]], [[the Bahamas]], the southern coast of [[Jamaica]], the western coast of [[Saint Lucia]], the [[Gulf of Paria]], the [[Great Sound]] and [[Castle Harbour, Bermuda|Castle Harbour]], [[Bermuda]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=50 Ships That Saved the World|last=Goodhart|first=Philip|publisher=Doubleday|year=1965|location=New York|pages=175}}</ref>

During the [[Second World War]], the United States deployed troops to fight in [[European theatre of World War II|Europe]], [[Mediterranean and Middle East theatre of World War II|North Africa]], and the [[Pacific War|Pacific]]. The U.S. was a key participant in many battles, including the [[Battle of Midway]], [[Operation Torch]], the [[Normandy landings]], and the [[Battle of the Bulge]]. In the time period between [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|December 7, 1941]], to [[Surrender of Japan|September 2, 1945]], more than 400,000 Americans were killed in the conflict. After the war, American and [[Allies of World War II|Allied]] troops occupied [[Allied-occupied Austria|Austria]], [[Allied-occupied Germany|Germany]] and [[Occupation of Japan|Japan]]. The U.S. maintains garrisoned military forces in both [[List of United States Army installations in Germany|Germany]] and [[United States Forces Japan|Japan]] today. The United States also gave economic support to a large number of countries and movements who were opposed to the [[Axis powers]]. President [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]]'s [[Cash and carry (World War II)|cash and carry]] policy was a precursor to what would become the [[Lend-Lease]] program, which "lent" a wide array of resources and weapons to many countries, especially Great Britain and the [[USSR]], ostensibly to be repaid after the war. In practice, the United States frequently either did not push for repayment or "sold" the goods for a nominal price, such as 10% of their value. Significant aid was also sent to France and Taiwan, and [[Resistance during World War II|resistance]] movements in countries [[German-occupied Europe|occupied]] by the Axis.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Ebbert, Jean |author2=Marie-Beth Hall |author3=Beach, Edward Latimer | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=hUoIaQqipboC&pg=PA28 | title= Crossed Currents| page= 28| isbn= 9781574881936 | year= 1999 |publisher=Brassey's }}</ref>

During the war, postwar planning efforts moved from securing a "quarter hemisphere" against Nazi Germany in June 1940<ref>Wertheim 54-71; Grand Area conceptualized by October 1940</ref> to economically and then politically and militarily dominating "the whole postwar world unified under U.S. leadership. Now globalization was axiomatic, requiring no justification. American interests and responsibilities "embrace the whole world."<ref>Wertheim 136.</ref> By early 1942, the diplomats and experts recruited by the [[United States Department of State]] saw the aim of U.S. superiority as a "established fact".

== Cold War ==
{{Covert United States involvement in regime change}}
{{Further|Military history of the United States#Cold War era (1945–1991)|United States involvement in regime change#1945–1991: Cold War}}
{{See also|U.S. policy towards authoritarianism|Domino theory}}
Following the Second World War, the U.S. spent billions to rebuild post-war Europe and aid global development through initiatives such as the [[Marshall Plan]]. The U.S. also helped form the [[North Atlantic Treaty Organization]] (NATO) in 1949 to resist communist expansion and supported resistance movements and dissidents in the communist regimes of Central and Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union during a period known as the [[Cold War]]. One example is the [[counterespionage]] operations following the discovery of the [[Farewell Dossier]] which some argue contributed to the fall of the Soviet regime.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna4394002 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040229021948/http://www.msnbc.msn.com/id/4394002/ |url-status=live |archive-date=2004-02-29 |title=CIA slipped bugs to Soviets |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |publisher=[[NBC]] |access-date=2008-11-21}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/csi-studies/studies/96unclass/farewell.htm |title=The Farewell Dossier |publisher=[[Central Intelligence Agency]] |access-date=2008-11-21 |archive-date=October 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191027171324/https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/csi-studies/studies/96unclass/farewell.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> After [[Joseph Stalin]] instituted the [[Berlin Blockade]],<ref>{{Harvnb|Gaddis|2005|p=33}}</ref> the United States, Britain, France, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and several other countries began the massive "[[Berlin airlift]]", supplying [[West Berlin]] with up to 4,700 tons of daily necessities.<ref name="Nash, Gary B 2008">Nash, Gary B. "The Next Steps: The Marshall Plan, NATO, and NSC-68." The American People: Creating a Nation and a Society. New York: Pearson Longman, 2008. P 828.</ref> [[United States Air Force|U.S. Air Force]] pilot [[Gail Halvorsen]] created "[[Operation Vittles]]", which supplied candy to German children.<ref name="miller26">{{Harvnb|Miller|2000|p=26}}</ref> In May 1949, Stalin backed down and lifted the blockade.<ref name="Gaddis 2005, p. 34">{{Harvnb|Gaddis|2005|p=34}}</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|Miller|2000|pp=180–81}}</ref>

[[File:USFK Logo.svg|thumb|left|[[United States Forces Korea]] was established in 1957 and oversees a contingent of ~24,000 U.S. troops in [[South Korea]] today.]]
In 1945, the United States and Soviet Union occupied Korea to disarm the [[Imperial Japanese Armed Forces]] that [[Korea under Japanese rule|occupied the Korean peninsula]]. The U.S. and Soviet Union split the country at the [[38th parallel north|38th parallel]] and each installed a government, with the Soviet Union installing a Stalinist [[Kim Il Sung]] in North Korea and the US supporting anti-communist [[Syngman Rhee]] in South Korea, who was elected president in 1948. Both leaders were authoritarian dictators. Tensions between the North and South erupted into [[Korean War|full-scale war]] in 1950 when North Korean forces invaded the South. From 1950 to 1953, U.S. and [[United Nations]] forces fought communist Chinese and North Korean troops in the war. The war resulted in 36,574 American deaths and 2–3 million Korean deaths. The war ended in a stalemate with the [[Korean Peninsula]] devastated and every major city in ruins. North Korea was among the most heavily bombed countries in history. Fighting ended on 27 July 1953 when an [[Korean Armistice Agreement|armistice]] was signed. The agreement created the [[Korean Demilitarized Zone]] (DMZ) to separate North and South Korea, and allowed the return of prisoners. However, because an armistice is only a temporary cessation of hostilities, and a peace treaty was never signed, the two Koreas are technically still at war. [[United States Forces Korea|U.S. troops have remained in South Korea]] with the stated aim of deterring further conflict.<ref name="Lewy pp. 450-453">{{cite book|last=Lewy|first=Guenter|author-link=Guenter Lewy|title=America in Vietnam|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|year=1980|isbn=978-0-19-987423-1|pages=450–453|quote=For the Korean War the only hard statistic is that of American military deaths, which included 33,629 battle deaths and 20,617 who died of other causes. The North Korean and Chinese Communists never published statistics of their casualties. The number of South Korean military deaths has been given as in excess of 400,000; the South Korean Ministry of Defense puts the number of killed and missing at 281,257. Estimates of communist troops killed are about one-half million. The total number of Korean civilians who died in the fighting, which left almost every major city in North and South Korea in ruins, has been estimated at between 2 and 3 million. This adds up to almost 1&nbsp;million military deaths and a possible 2.5&nbsp;million civilians who were killed or died as a result of this extremely destructive conflict. |title-link=America in Vietnam}}</ref>

{{See also|Five Eyes|U.S. Army and CIA interrogation manuals|Plausible deniability}}
Throughout the Cold War, the U.S. frequently used government agencies such as the [[National Security Agency]] (NSA) and the [[Central Intelligence Agency]] (CIA) for [[Covert operation|covert]] and [[clandestine operations]] against governments, groups, and individuals considered unfriendly to U.S. interests, especially in the Middle East, Latin America, and Africa. In 1949, during the [[Presidency of Harry S. Truman|Truman administration]], a [[March 1949 Syrian coup d'état|coup d'état]] overthrew an elected parliamentary government in [[First Syrian Republic|Syria]], which had delayed approving an oil pipeline requested by U.S. international business interests in that region. The exact role of the CIA in the coup is controversial, but it is clear that U.S. governmental officials, including at least one CIA officer, communicated with [[Husni al-Za'im]], the coup's organizer, prior to the March 30 coup, and were at least aware that it was being planned. Six weeks later, on May 16, Za'im approved the pipeline.<ref>{{cite book|last=Wilford|first=Hugh|title=America's Great Game: The CIA's Secret Arabists and the Making of the Modern Middle East|publisher=Basic Books|year=2013|isbn=978-0-465-01965-6|pages=[https://archive.org/details/americasgreatgam0000wilf/page/94 94, 101]|url=https://archive.org/details/americasgreatgam0000wilf/page/94}}</ref>

From 1949 to 1956, NATO unsuccessfully attempted to [[Operation Valuable|overthrow]] Albania's [[People's Socialist Republic of Albania|communist regime]]. After their defeat in the [[Chinese Civil War]], parts of the [[Kuomintang in Burma|Nationalist army]] retreated south and crossed the border into Burma.<ref name=":Han">{{Cite book |last=Han |first=Enze |title=The Ripple Effect: China's Complex Presence in Southeast Asia |date=2024 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-769659-0 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>{{Rp|page=65}} The United States supported these Nationalist forces because the United States hoped they would harass the People's Republic of China from the [[Southwestern China|southwest]], thereby diverting Chinese resources from the [[Korean War]].<ref name=":Han" />{{Rp|page=65}} The Burmese government protested and international pressure increased.<ref name=":Han" />{{Rp|page=65}} Beginning in 1953, several rounds of withdrawals of the Nationalist forces and their families were carried out.<ref name=":Han" />{{Rp|page=65}} In [[1960–61 campaign at the China–Burma border|1960, joint military action]] by China and Burma expelled the remaining Nationalist forces from Burma, although [[Kuomintang Chinese in Thailand|some went on to settle]] in the [[Myanmar–Thailand border|Burma-Thailand borderlands]].<ref name=":Han" />{{Rp|pages=65–66}}

[[File:59mossadeghprime minister1951.jpg|thumb|The U.S. orchestrated the [[1953 Iranian coup d'état#United States' role|1953 Iranian coup d'état]] which ousted Prime Minister [[Mohammad Mosaddegh]].]]
[[File:Reforma agraria 1952.jpg|thumb|When democratically elected Guatemalan President [[Jacobo Árbenz]] attempted a modest [[Decree 900|redistribution of land]], he was overthrown in the [[1954 Guatemalan coup d'état|1954 CIA Guatemalan coup d'état]].]]
In the early 1950s, the CIA spearheaded [[Project FF]], a clandestine effort to pressure the Egyptian king [[Farouk of Egypt|Farouk I]] into embracing political reforms amenable to American interests. After he resisted, the project shifted towards deposing him, and Farouk was subsequently overthrown in a [[1952 Egyptian revolution|military coup]] in 1952.<ref name=holland>{{cite book |last1=Holland |first1=Matthew F. |date=July 11, 1996 |publisher=Praeger|title=America and Egypt: From Roosevelt to Eisenhower |isbn=978-0-275-95474-1 |pages=27}}</ref> In 1953, under U.S. President [[Dwight Eisenhower]], the CIA helped [[Shah]] [[Mohammad Reza Pahlavi]] of [[Iran]] [[1953 Iranian coup d'état|remove]] the democratically elected Prime Minister, [[Mohammad Mosaddegh]]. Supporters of U.S. policy claimed that Mossadegh had ended democracy through a rigged referendum.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/library/world/mideast/041600iran-cia-index.html |work=The New York Times |title=New York Times Special Report: The C.I.A. in Iran}}</ref> [[Allen Dulles]] oversaw the CIA's covert operations beginning in 1951 and in 1953 became the CIA's first civilian director, overseeing many covert operations until his dismissal in 1961.

In 1952, the CIA launched [[Operation PBFortune]] and, in 1954, [[1954 Guatemalan coup d'état|Operation PBSuccess]] to [[Deposition (politics)|depose]] the democratically elected [[President of Guatemala|Guatemalan President]] [[Jacobo Árbenz]] and ended the [[Guatemalan Revolution]]. The coup installed the military dictatorship of [[Carlos Castillo Armas]], the first in a series of U.S.-backed dictators who ruled Guatemala. Guatemala subsequently plunged into a [[Guatemalan Civil War|civil war]] that cost thousands of lives and ended all democratic expression for decades.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/theguardian/2007/feb/02/features11.g2 |location=London |work=The Guardian |first=Billy |last=Briggs |title=Billy Briggs on the atrocities of Guatemala's civil war |date=2 February 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/americas/country_profiles/1215811.stm |work=BBC News |title=Timeline: Guatemala |date=9 November 2011}}</ref><ref>CDI:  The Center for Defense Information, The Defense Monitor, "The World At War: January 1, 1998".</ref>

The CIA armed an indigenous insurgency in order to oppose the [[Battle of Chamdo|invasion]] and subsequent [[History of Tibet (1950–present)|control of Tibet]] by China<ref>Conboy, Kenneth and Morrison, James, ''The CIA's Secret War in Tibet'' (2002).</ref> and sponsored [[Permesta|a failed revolt]] against [[President of Indonesia|Indonesian President]] [[Sukarno]] in 1958.<ref>{{cite book
  |last = Road night
  |first = Andrew
  |title = United States Policy towards Indonesia in the Truman and Eisenhower Years
  |publisher = Palgrave Macmillan
  |year = 2002
  |location = New York
  |isbn = 0-333-79315-3}}</ref> As part of the [[Eisenhower Doctrine]], the U.S. also deployed troops to Lebanon in [[Operation Blue Bat]]. President Eisenhower also imposed [[United States embargo against Cuba|embargoes on Cuba]] in 1958. Covert operations continued under President [[John F. Kennedy]] and his successors. In 1961, the CIA attempted to depose Cuban president [[Fidel Castro]] through the [[Bay of Pigs Invasion]]; however the invasion failed when President Kennedy withdrew overt U.S. air support at the last minute. During [[Operation Mongoose]], the CIA aggressively pursued its efforts to overthrow [[Political career of Fidel Castro|Castro's regime]] by [[CIA assassination attempts on Fidel Castro|conducting various assassination attempts]] on him and facilitating U.S.-sponsored [[United States and state-sponsored terrorism|terrorist]] attacks in Cuba. American efforts to sabotage Cuba's national security played a significant role in the events leading up to the [[Cuban Missile Crisis]], which saw the U.S. blockade the island during a confrontation with the Soviet Union. The CIA also considered assassinating Congolese leader [[Patrice Lumumba]] with poisoned toothpaste (although this plan was aborted).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.history-matters.com/archive/church/reports/ir/pdf/ChurchIR_3A_Congo.pdf|title=ASSASSINATION PLANNING AND THE PLOTS A. CONGO }}</ref><ref name="cyoung">{{cite journal |title = Post-Independence Politics in the Congo |author = M. Crawford Young |journal = Transition |year = 1966 |issue = 26 |jstor = 2934325 |pages=34–41|doi = 10.2307/2934325 }}</ref><ref>Gott 2004 p. 219.</ref>

In 1961, the CIA sponsored the assassination of [[Rafael Trujillo]], former dictator of the Dominican Republic.<ref name="NSAEBB222-1973-05-08">{{citation
 |url = http://www.gwu.edu/~nsarchiv/NSAEBB/NSAEBB222/index.htm
 |volume = George Washington University National Security Archives Electronic Briefing Book No. 222, ''The CIA's Family Jewels''
 |title = Memorandum for the Executive Secretary, CIA Management Committee. Subject: Potentially Embarrassing Agency Activities
 |editor = Blanton, William
 |date =  8 May 1973
}}</ref> After a period of instability, U.S. troops intervened in the Dominican Republic during the [[Dominican Civil War]] (April 1965) to prevent a takeover by supporters of deposed left wing president [[Juan Bosch (politician)|Juan Bosch]] who were fighting supporters of General [[Elías Wessin y Wessin]]. The soldiers were also deployed to evacuate foreign citizens. The U.S. deployed 22,000 soldiers and 44 died. The [[Organization of American States|OAS]] also deployed soldiers to the conflict through the [[Inter-American Peace Force]]. U.S. soldiers were gradually withdrawn from May onwards. The war officially ended on September 3, 1965. The first [[1966 Dominican Republic general election|postwar elections]] were held on July 1, 1966. Conservative [[Joaquín Balaguer]] defeated former president Juan Bosch.<ref name=McFarland>{{cite book|last1=De La Pedraja|first1=René|title=Wars of Latin America, 1948–1982: The Rise of the Guerrillas|date=2013-04-15|publisher=McFarland|page=149}}</ref>

[[File:Kennedy and Jagan 1961.jpg|thumb|right|President [[John F. Kennedy]] meeting with [[Cheddi Jagan]] in October 1961. The trip was a political disaster for Jagan, who failed to sooth the suspicions of Kennedy and Congress by equivocating on Cold War issues.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Rabe|first1=Stephen G.|author-link=Stephen G. Rabe|title=The Most Dangerous Area in the World: John F. Kennedy Confronts Communist Revolution in Latin America|date=1999|publisher=University of North Carolina press|location=Chapel Hill|isbn=0-8078-4764-X|pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=hVhuAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA86 86–88]}}</ref>]]
At the end of the [[Eisenhower]] administration, a campaign was initiated to deny [[Cheddi Jagan]] power in an independent [[Guyana]].{{sfn|Rabe|2005|pages=72–73}} This campaign was intensified and became something of an obsession of [[John F. Kennedy]], because he feared a "second Cuba".{{sfn|Rabe|2005|pages=8, 123}} By the time Kennedy took office, the United Kingdom was ready to decolonize [[British Guiana]] and did not fear Jagan's political leanings, yet chose to cooperate in the plot for the sake of good relations with the United States.{{sfn|Rabe|2005|page=177}} The CIA cooperated with [[AFL-CIO]], most notably in organizing an 80-day general strike in 1963, backing it up with a strike fund estimated to be over $1 million.{{sfn|Rabe|2005|pages=110–112}} The Kennedy Administration put pressure on [[Harold Macmillan]]'s government to help in its effort, ultimately attaining a promise in July 1963, that Macmillan's government would unseat Jagan.{{sfn|Rabe|2005|page=118}}

This was achieved through a plan developed by [[Duncan Sandys]] whereby Sandys, after feigning impartiality in a Guyanese dispute, would decide in favor of [[Forbes Burnham]] and [[Peter D'Aguiar]], calling for new elections based on [[proportional representation]] before independence would be considered, under which Jagan's opposition would have better chances to win.{{sfn|Rabe|2005|pages=106, 119–122}} The plan succeeded, and the Burnham-D'Aguiar coalition took power soon after winning [[1964 British Guiana general election|the election]] in December 1964.{{sfn|Rabe|2005||page=137}} The [[Lyndon B. Johnson|Johnson]] administration later helped Burnham fix the [[1968 Guyanese general election|fraudulent 1968 election]]—the first election after decolonization in 1966.{{sfn|Rabe|2005|pages=157–160}} To guarantee Burnham's victory, Johnson also approved a well-timed [[Food for Peace]] loan, announced some weeks before the election so as to influence the election but not to appear to be doing so.{{sfn|Rabe|2005|pages=157–160}} [[Guyana–United States relations|U.S.–Guyanese relations]] cooled in the [[Richard Nixon|Nixon]] administration. [[Henry Kissinger]], in his memoirs, dismissed Guyana as being "invariably on the side of radicals in Third World forums."{{sfn|Rabe|2005|pages=168–169}}

{{See also|DESOTO patrol|MACV-SOG}}
From 1965 to 1973, U.S. troops fought at the request of [[South Vietnam]], [[Kingdom of Laos|Laos]], and [[Kingdom of Cambodia (1953–1970)|Cambodia]] during the [[Vietnam War]] against the [[Vietnam People's Armed Forces|military of North Vietnam]], [[Viet Cong]], [[Pathet Lao]], [[China]], [[Soviet Union]], [[North Korea]] and [[Khmer Rouge]] insurgents. President [[Lyndon Johnson]] escalated U.S. involvement following the [[Gulf of Tonkin Resolution]]. North Vietnam [[North Vietnamese invasion of Laos|invaded]] Laos in 1959, and used 30,000 men to build invasion routes through Laos and Cambodia.<ref name="The Economist February 26, 1983">''The Economist'', February 26, 1983.{{title?}}</ref> North Vietnam sent 10,000 troops to attack the south in 1964, and this figure increased to 100,000 in 1965.<ref name="Washington Post, April 23, 1985">''Washington Post'', April 23, 1985.{{title?}}</ref> By early 1965, 7,559 South Vietnamese hamlets had been destroyed by the Viet Cong.<ref>''Reader's Digest,'' [http://www.paulbogdanor.com/left/vietnam/hochiminh.html "The Blood-Red Hands of Ho Chi Minh"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210811170309/http://www.paulbogdanor.com/left/vietnam/hochiminh.html |date=August 11, 2021 }}, November 1968.</ref> The CIA organized [[Hmong people]] to fight against the Pathet Lao, and used [[Air America (airline)|Air America]] to "drop 46 million pounds of foodstuffs....transport tens of thousands of troops, conduct a highly successful photoreconnaissance program, and engage in numerous clandestine missions using night-vision glasses and state-of-the-art electronic equipment."<ref>{{cite web|author=Leary, William M. |title=CIA Air Operations in Laos, 1955–1974.|website=CIA|date=June 27, 2008|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/csi-studies/studies/winter99-00/art7.html|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20201128021711/https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/csi-studies/studies/winter99-00/art7.html|archivedate=2020-11-28|url-status=dead}}</ref>

After sponsoring a [[1963 South Vietnamese coup d'état|coup]] against [[Ngô Đình Diệm]], the CIA was asked "to coax a genuine South Vietnamese government into being" by managing development and running the [[Phoenix Program]] that killed thousands of insurgents. In 1968, [[Chief of Staff of the United States Army|U.S. Army Chief of Staff]] [[William Westmoreland]] also sought to put [[Fracture Jaw|nuclear weapons in South Vietnam]], but the project was abandoned in February of the same year after public statements by [[Eugene McCarthy]] and others revealed its plans to the public.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sanger |first=David E. |date=2018-10-06 |title=U.S. General Considered Nuclear Response in Vietnam War, Cables Show |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/10/06/world/asia/vietnam-war-nuclear-weapons.html |access-date=2024-02-25 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US }}</ref> North Vietnamese forces attempted to overrun Cambodia in 1970,<ref>Dmitry Mosyakov, "The Khmer Rouge and the Vietnamese Communists: A History of Their Relations as Told in the Soviet Archives," in Susan E. Cook, ed., ''Genocide in Cambodia and Rwanda'' (Yale Genocide Studies Program Monograph Series No. 1, 2004), p54ff. "In April–May 1970, many North Vietnamese forces entered Cambodia in response to the call for help addressed to Vietnam not by Pol Pot, but by his deputy Nuon Chea. Nguyen Co Thach recalls: "Nuon Chea has asked for help and we have liberated five provinces of Cambodia in ten days."</ref> to which the U.S. and South Vietnam responded with a [[Cambodian campaign|limited incursion]].<ref name="The Economist February 26, 1983" /><ref name="Washington Post, April 23, 1985" /><ref>[[Peter Rodman|Rodman, Peter]], [http://www.brookings.edu/opinions/2007/0823iraq_rodman.aspx Returning to Cambodia], Brookings Institution, August 23, 2007.</ref> The U.S. bombing of Cambodia, called [[Operation Menu]], proved controversial. Although David Chandler argued that the bombing "had the effect the Americans wanted--it broke the communist encirclement of [[Phnom Penh]],"<ref>Chandler, David 2000, Brother Number One: A Political Biography of Pol Pot, Revised Edition, Chiang Mai, Thailand: Silkworm Books, pp. 96-7.</ref> others have claimed it boosted recruitment for the Khmer Rouge.<ref>{{cite book |author=Shawcross, William |title=Sideshow: Kissinger, Nixon and the Destruction of Cambodia |publisher=University of Michigan |year=1979 |isbn= 0-671-23070-0 }}</ref> North Vietnam violated the [[Paris Peace Accords]] after the US withdrew, and all of Indochina had fallen to communist governments by late 1975.

{{See also|POMCUS|Exercise Reforger}}

[[File:Pinochet Aylwin Bush.png|thumb|left|Chilean General [[Augusto Pinochet]] with [[George H. W. Bush]]]]
In 1975, it was revealed by the [[Church Committee]] that the [[United States intervention in Chile|United States had covertly intervened in Chile]] from as early as 1962, and that from 1963 to 1973, covert involvement was "extensive and continuous".<ref>{{cite web|author=Church Committee|author-link=Church Committee|url=https://archive.org/details/Covert-Action-In-Chile-1963-1973|title=Covert Action in Chile: 1963–1973|date=1975|pages=[https://archive.org/stream/Covert-Action-In-Chile-1963-1973/94chile#page/n17/mode/2up 14–15], [https://archive.org/stream/Covert-Action-In-Chile-1963-1973/94chile#page/n4/mode/1up 1]}}</ref> In 1970, at the request of President [[Richard Nixon]], the CIA planned a "constitutional coup" to prevent the election of Marxist leader [[Salvador Allende]] in Chile, while secretly encouraging [[Chilean Armed Forces]] generals to act against him.<ref name="Falcoff 2003">{{cite web|authorlink=Mark Falcoff|last=Falcoff|first=Mark|url=https://www.commentary.org/articles/mark-falcoff/kissinger-chile-the-myth-that-will-not-die/|title=Kissinger & Chile: The Myth That Will Not Die|work=[[Commentary (magazine)|Commentary]]|date=November 2003|accessdate=2025-10-25}}</ref> The CIA changed its approach after the murder of Chilean general [[René Schneider]].<ref name="Interim Report">[http://history-matters.com/archive/church/reports/ir/contents.htm Alleged Assassination Plots Involving Foreign Leaders (1975)], [[Church Committee]], pages 246–247 and 250–254.</ref> Although disputed by [[Mark Falcoff]],<ref name="Falcoff 2003"/> [[Peter Kornbluh]] and other analysts state that the CIA destabilized Chile and helped create the conditions for the [[1973 Chilean coup d'état]], which led to years of dictatorship under [[Augusto Pinochet]].<ref name="The Pinochet File">{{cite book|last=Kornbluh|first=Peter|title=The Pinochet File: A Declassified Dossier on Atrocity and Accountability|year=2003|publisher=The New Press|location=New York|isbn=1-56584-936-1}}</ref>

From October 1972 to March 1975, the CIA armed [[Kurdistan Democratic Party|Kurdish rebels]] fighting the [[Ba'athist Iraq|Ba'athist government of Iraq]]. The Kurds suffered a total defeat after [[1975 Algiers Agreement|Iran and Iraq agreed to resolve their border dispute]], leading to a cessation of U.S., Israeli, and Iranian sponsorship.<ref>{{cite book|last=Gibson|first=Bryan R.|title=Sold Out? US Foreign Policy, Iraq, the Kurds, and the Cold War|publisher=[[Palgrave Macmillan]]|year=2015|isbn=978-1-137-48711-7|pages=140, 144–145, 148, 181, 186, 190–191, 194–195, 204–205}}</ref> In 1973, Nixon authorized [[Operation Nickel Grass]], an overt strategic airlift to deliver weapons and supplies to [[Israel]] during the [[Yom Kippur War]], after the Soviet Union began sending arms to Syria and Egypt. The same year, [[Libya]]n leader [[Muammar Gaddafi]] claimed the [[Gulf of Sidra]] as sovereign territory and closed the bay, prompting the U.S. to conduct [[freedom of navigation]] operations in the area, as it saw Libya's claims as [[Convention on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone|internationally illegitimate]]. The dispute resulted in Libyan-U.S. confrontations, including an [[Gulf of Sidra incident (1981)|incident in 1981]] in which two U.S. [[Grumman F-14 Tomcat|F-14 Tomcats]] shot down two Libyan [[Sukhoi Su-17|Su-22 Fitters]] over the gulf. In response to purported Libyan involvement in international [[State terrorism|terrorism]], specifically the [[1985 Rome and Vienna airport attacks]], the [[Presidency of Ronald Reagan|Reagan administration]] launched Operation Attain Document in early 1986,<ref>{{cite web |title=Operation Attain Document |url=https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/ops/attain_document.htm |access-date=January 16, 2022 |work=Global Security}}</ref> which saw [[Action in the Gulf of Sidra (1986)|operations in March 1986]] that killed 72 Libyans and destroyed multiple boats and [[Surface-to-air missile|SAM]] sites. In April 1986, the U.S. [[1986 United States bombing of Libya|bombed Libya]] again, killing over 40 Libyan soldiers and up to 30 civilians. The U.S. [[1989 air battle near Tobruk|shot down]] two [[Libyan Air Force]] MiG-23 fighters 40 miles (64&nbsp;km) north of [[Tobruk]] in 1989.<ref>{{cite book|last=Lehman|first=John F.|orig-year= 1988|title=Command of the Seas|publisher=Naval Institute Press|location =Annapolis|year=2001|page=351|isbn= 978-1-55750-534-7}}</ref><ref>Stanik, Joseph T. (2003). ''El Dorado Canyon: Reagan's Undeclared War with Qaddafi''. Naval Institute Press. p. 29. {{ISBN|978-1-55750-983-3}}.</ref>

Months after the [[Saur Revolution]] brought a communist regime to power in Afghanistan, the U.S. began offering limited financial aid to Afghan dissidents through Pakistan's [[Inter-Services Intelligence]], although the [[Carter administration]] rejected Pakistani requests to provide arms.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N_hfPrIMYuEC&q=afghanistan |title=From the Shadows: The Ultimate Insider's Story of Five Presidents and How They Won the Cold War |author=Robert M. Gates |page=146 |date=2007 |publisher=Simon Schuster |isbn=978-1-4165-4336-7 |access-date=July 28, 2011}}</ref> After the [[Iranian Revolution]], the United States sought rapprochement with the Afghan government—a prospect that the USSR found unacceptable due to the weakening Soviet leverage over the regime.<ref>Rubin, Michael, [http://meria.idc.ac.il/journal/2002/issue1/mrubin.pdf "Who is Responsible for the Taliban?"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210924045209/http://meria.idc.ac.il/journal/2002/issue1/mrubin.pdf |date=September 24, 2021 }}, ''Middle East Review of International Affairs'', Vol. 6, No. 1 (March 2002).</ref> The Soviets [[Soviet–Afghan War|invaded]] Afghanistan in December 1979 to depose [[Hafizullah Amin]] and install a [[puppet regime]] led by [[Babrak Karmal]]. Disgusted by the collapse of [[détente]], President [[Jimmy Carter]] began covertly arming Afghan [[mujahideen]] in a program called [[Operation Cyclone]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Coll|first=Steve|title=[[Ghost Wars|Ghost Wars: The Secret History of the CIA, Afghanistan, and Bin Laden, from the Soviet Invasion to September 10, 2001]]|publisher=[[Penguin Group]]|year=2004|isbn=9781594200076|page=[https://archive.org/details/ghostwarssecreth00coll/page/58 58]|author-link=Steve Coll|quote=The CIA's mission was spelled out in an amended Top Secret presidential finding signed by President Carter in late December 1979 and reauthorized by President Reagan in 1981. The finding permitted the CIA to ship weapons secretly to the mujahedin. The document used the word ''harassment'' to describe the CIA's goals against Soviet forces. The CIA's covert action was to raise the cost of Soviet intervention in Afghanistan. It might also deter the Soviets from undertaking other Third World invasions. But this was not a war the CIA expected to win outright on the battlefield.}}</ref>

[[File:82nd Airborne soldiers on Grenada 1983.jpg|thumb|[[82nd Airborne Division|82nd Airborne]] soldiers during [[United States invasion of Grenada|Operation Urgent Fury]], the American invasion of [[Grenada]] in October 1983]]
Operation Cyclone was greatly expanded under President [[Ronald Reagan]] as part of the [[Reagan Doctrine]]. In accordance to this doctrine, the CIA also supported the [[UNITA]] movement in [[Angola]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.globalsecurity.org/military/world/para/unita.htm|title=UNITA Uniao Nacional para a Independecia Total de Angola|author=John Pike|work=globalsecurity.org}}</ref> the [[Solidarity (Polish trade union)|Solidarity]] movement in [[Poland]],<ref>MacEachin, Douglas J. [https://web.archive.org/web/20070613085810/https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/books-and-monographs/us-intelligence-and-the-polish-crisis-1980-1981/index.htm "US Intelligence and the Polish Crisis 1980-1981."] CIA. June 28, 2008.</ref> the [[Contras]] in [[Nicaragua]], and the [[Khmer People's National Liberation Front]] in [[Cambodia]].<ref>[http://www.worldandi.com/specialreport/1988/february/Sa13957.htm "Cambodia at a Crossroads"], by Michael Johns, ''The World and I'' magazine, February 1988</ref><ref>Far Eastern Economic Review, December 22, 1988,{{title?}} details the extensive fighting between the U.S.-backed forces and the Khmer Rouge.{{verify source|date=January 2026}}</ref> U.S. and UN forces later supervised free elections in Cambodia.<ref name="UN_SRES7451992">{{UN document |docid=S-RES-745(1992) |type=Resolution |body=Security Council |year=1992 |resolution_number=745 |accessdate=2008-04-09|date=28 February 1992}}</ref> Under Reagan, the US sent troops to [[Lebanon]] during the [[Lebanese Civil War]] as part of a peace-keeping mission, later withdrawing after 241 servicemen were killed in the [[Beirut barracks bombing]]. In [[Operation Earnest Will]], U.S. warships escorted reflagged [[Kuwait]]i oil tankers to protect them from Iranian attacks during the [[Iran–Iraq War]]. The United States Navy launched [[Operation Praying Mantis]] in retaliation for the Iranian [[naval mine|mining]] of the [[Persian Gulf]] during the war and the subsequent damage to an American warship. The attack helped pressure Iran to agree to a ceasefire with Iraq later that summer, ending the eight-year war.<ref>{{cite book|author=Peniston, Bradley|title=No Higher Honor: Saving the USS Samuel B. Roberts in the Persian Gulf |url=http://www.navybook.com/nohigherhonor|location=Annapolis |publisher=Naval Institute Press|year=2006|isbn=1-59114-661-5}}, p. 217.</ref>

Under Carter and Reagan, the CIA repeatedly intervened to prevent right-wing coups in El Salvador and the U.S. frequently threatened aid suspensions to curtail government atrocities in the [[Salvadoran Civil War]]. As a result, the [[Death squads in El Salvador|death squads]] made plans to kill the U.S. Ambassador.<ref>''Washington Post'', February 24, July 13, 1980 (Carter); ''New York Times'', November 20, 26, December 12, 1983 (Reagan); ''New York Times'', June 24, 1984, Washington Post, June 27, 1984 (Ambassador)</ref> In 1983, after an internal power struggle ended with the [[Deposition (politics)|deposition]] and murder of revolutionary Prime Minister [[Maurice Bishop]], the U.S. invaded [[Grenada]] in [[Operation Urgent Fury]] and held free elections. In 1989, President [[George H. W. Bush]] ordered an [[United States invasion of Panama|invasion of Panama]] to depose dictator [[Manuel Noriega]] in [[Operation Nifty Package]]. Noriega had been giving [[military aid]] to [[Contras|Contra groups]] in Nicaragua at the request of the US, which in turn tolerated his drug trafficking activities, known since the 1960s. Under Bush, the CIA provided Noriega with hundreds of thousands of dollars for his assistance to the groups. The DEA was eventually permitted to indict him for drug trafficking after documents regarding the [[CIA activities in Nicaragua]] fell into the hands of the [[Sandinistas]]. He surrendered to US soldiers on January 3, 1990, and was sentenced by a US court to 45 years in prison.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cnn.com/2010/CRIME/04/27/noriega.extradition/index.html |publisher=CNN |title=Noriega extradited to France |date=26 April 2010 |access-date=August 5, 2011 |archive-date=October 10, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121010053059/http://articles.cnn.com/2010-04-27/justice/noriega.extradition_1_manuel-noriega-noriega-s-extradition-new-trial?_s=PM:CRIME |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Post-Cold War ==
{{Further|United States involvement in regime change#1991–present: Post-Cold War}}
[[File:Demolished vehicles line Highway 80 on 18 Apr 1991.jpg|thumb|left|Destroyed vehicles along the [[Highway of Death]] in 1991, a legacy of the [[Gulf War]]]]
In 1990 and 1991, the U.S. intervened in [[Kuwait]] after a series of failed diplomatic negotiations, and led a coalition to repel [[Iraqi invasion of Kuwait|invading Iraqi forces]] led by dictator [[Saddam Hussein]], in what became known as the [[Gulf War]]. In February 1991, the coalition succeeded in driving out the Iraqi forces. The U.S., UK, and France responded to popular Shia and Kurdish demands for [[Iraqi no-fly zones conflict|no-fly zones]], and [[Gulf War#Military means|intervened]] by enforcing them in Iraq's south and north to protect the Shia and Kurdish populations from Saddam's regime. The no-fly zones cut off Saddam from the country's Kurdish north, effectively granting autonomy to the Kurds, and would stay active for 12 years until the [[2003 invasion of Iraq]]. In the 1990s, the U.S. intervened in Somalia as part of [[United Nations Operation in Somalia I|UNOSOM I]] and [[United Nations Operation in Somalia II|UNOSOM II]], a United Nations humanitarian relief operation<ref>Christiane E. Philipp, ''Somalia – A Very Special Case'' (2005), Max Planck Yearbook of United Nations Law</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://peacekeeping.un.org/mission/past/unosom1backgr2.html|title=Somalia - UNOSOM I|publisher=United Nations Peacekeeping|access-date=January 6, 2026}}</ref>

During the [[Battle of Mogadishu (1993)]], [[MH-60 Black Hawk|two U.S. helicopters]] were shot down by [[rocket-propelled grenade]] attacks to their [[tail rotor]]s, trapping soldiers behind enemy lines. This resulted in a brief but bitter street firefight; 18 Americans and more than 300 Somalis were killed. Under President [[Bill Clinton]], the U.S. participated in [[Operation Uphold Democracy]], a [[United Nations|UN]] mission to reinstate the elected [[president of Haiti]], [[Jean-Bertrand Aristide]], after a military coup.<ref>John R. Ballard, ''Upholding Democracy: The United States Military Campaign in Haiti, 1994–1997'' (1998)</ref> In 1995, the U.S. and [[NATO]] militarily intervened in [[Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina|Bosnia and Herzegovina]] against the [[Army of Republika Srpska]] as part of [[Operation Deliberate Force]], an air campaign aimed at halting attacks on [[United Nations Safe Areas|UN safe zones]] and civilians. Clinton deployed U.S. peacekeepers to Bosnia in late 1995, to uphold the subsequent [[Dayton Agreement]]. The CIA was involved in the failed [[CIA activities in Iraq|1996 coup attempt]] against Saddam Hussein.<ref>{{citation
 | url = http://www.afio.com/sections/wins/2003/2003-19.html#terrirst
 | author = Association of Former Intelligence Officers
 | title = US Coup Plotting in Iraq
 | id = Weekly Intelligence Notes 19-03
 | date = 19 May 2003
 | access-date = July 26, 2019
 | archive-date = November 22, 2021
 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20211122171009/https://www.afio.com/sections/wins/2003/2003-19.html#terrirst
 | url-status = dead
 }}</ref>

In December 1998, the U.S. and UK [[1998 bombing of Iraq|bombed]] Iraqi forces due to Iraq's failure to comply with UN inspectors searching for [[weapons of mass destruction]]. In response to the 1998 [[al-Qaeda]] [[1998 United States embassy bombings|bombings of U.S. embassies in East Africa]] that killed a dozen Americans and hundreds of Africans, President Clinton ordered [[Operation Infinite Reach]] on August 20, 1998, in which the U.S. Navy launched [[cruise missile]]s at al-Qaeda [[Afghan training camp|training camps]] in [[Afghanistan]] and a [[Al-Shifa pharmaceutical factory|pharmaceutical factory]] in [[Sudan]] believed to be producing [[VX (nerve agent)|chemical weapons]] for the terror group. It was the first publicly acknowledged [[preemptive strike]] against a [[violent non-state actor]] conducted by the U.S. military.<ref>{{cite web |first=John |last=Pike |url=http://www.globalsecurity.org/military/systems/munitions/bgm-109-operation.htm |title=BGM-109 Tomahawk – Smart Weapons |publisher=Globalsecurity.org |access-date=August 17, 2011}}</ref>

[[File:Нато бомбе изазивале еколошку катастрофу у Новом Саду.jpeg|thumb|right|U.S. forces participated in the 1999 NATO bombing of [[Serbia and Montenegro|Yugoslavia]].]]
The [[Police of Serbia]] and the [[Yugoslav Army (Federal Republic of Yugoslavia)|Yugoslav army]] carried out numerous [[war crimes in the Kosovo War]], including an [[ethnic cleansing]] of Albanians in the former [[Federal Republic of Yugoslavia]].<ref>Cohen, William (April 7, 1999). "Secretary Cohen's Press Conference at NATO Headquarters {{Cite web |url=http://www.defense.gov/transcripts/transcript.aspx?transcriptid=582 |title=Transcript |access-date=July 14, 2012 |archive-date=May 29, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110529025020/http://www.defense.gov/transcripts/transcript.aspx?transcriptid=582}}". Retrieved August 30, 2011.</ref><ref>Clinton, Bill (June 25, 1999). "[https://web.archive.org/web/20041109041056/http://clinton6.nara.gov/1999/06/1999-06-25-press-conference-by-the-president.html Press Conference by the President] ". Retrieved August 30, 2011.</ref> Several attempts were made by the UN and NATO to end the [[Kosovo War]], including the [[Rambouillet Agreement|Rabouillet Agreement]], but Yugoslavia refused to sign. As a result of the continued cleansing, [[NATO]] launched a bombing campaign against the country in 1999 with U.S. involvement, nicknamed [[Operation Allied Force]]. A 2016 study by [[Carnegie Mellon University]] professor Dov Levin found that the United States intervened in 81 foreign elections between 1946 and 2000, with the majority of those being through covert, rather than overt, actions.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Levin|first=Dov H.|title=When the Great Power Gets a Vote: The Effects of Great Power Electoral Interventions on Election Results|journal=[[International Studies Quarterly]]|volume=60|issue=2|date=June 2016|pages=189–202|doi=10.1093/isq/sqv016|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=X |date=2016-12-21 |title=The U.S. is no stranger to interfering in the elections of other countries |url=https://www.latimes.com/nation/la-na-us-intervention-foreign-elections-20161213-story.html |access-date=2024-08-20 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref> A 2021 review of the existing literature found that foreign interventions since World War II tend overwhelmingly to fail to achieve their purported objectives.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Malis |first1=Matt |last2=Querubin |first2=Pablo |last3=Satyanath |first3=Shanker |title=The Handbook of Historical Economics |chapter=Persistent failure? International interventions since World War II |date=2021 |pages=641–673 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-815874-6.00038-1 |isbn=978-0-12-815874-6 }}</ref>

== War on terror ==
{{Main|War on terror|United States foreign policy in the Middle East}}

{{See also|United States Department of State list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations|Specially Designated Global Terrorist|War Powers Resolution|Extraordinary rendition|CIA black sites}}
After the [[September 11 attacks]], under President [[George W. Bush]], the U.S. and NATO launched the global [[war on terror]]. Alongside conventional ground interventions, the war on terror saw the U.S. military and [[United States Intelligence Community|intelligence community]] evolve its [[asymmetric warfare]] capabilities, seeing the extensive usage of [[drone strike]]s and special operations in various foreign countries including [[List of drone strikes in Afghanistan|Afghanistan]], [[Drone strikes in Pakistan|Pakistan]], [[Drone strikes in Yemen|Yemen]], and [[American military intervention in Somalia (2007–present)|Somalia]] against suspected terrorist groups and their leadership.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Currier|first1=Cora|title=Everything We Know So Far About Drone Strikes|url=https://www.propublica.org/article/everything-we-know-so-far-about-drone-strikes|publisher=ProPublica|access-date=9 March 2017|language=en|date=5 February 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Drone Papers|url=https://theintercept.com/drone-papers/|website=The Intercept|access-date=9 March 2017}}</ref> The war on terror also continued the United States' legacy of waging [[undeclared war]]s, with the U.S. Congress only [[Declaration of war by the United States|formally declaring war]] 11 times as of September 2024, with the last declaration occurring in 1942 during the Second World War.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2013/08/all-the-previous-declarations-of-war/279246/|title=All the Previous Declarations of War|last=Franke-Ruta|first=Garance|date=31 August 2019|website=The Atlantic|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-01}}</ref>

=== Operation Enduring Freedom and Iraq invasion ===
{{See also|Authorization for Use of Military Force of 2001|Disposition Matrix|Special Operations Forces Liaison Element}}
[[File:SEAL conducting sensitive site exploitation mission in Jaji Mountains1.jpg|thumb|[[U.S. Navy SEALs]] in the Afghan mountains during the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)|War in Afghanistan]], January 2002]]
The war on terror began in earnest when the U.S. [[United States invasion of Afghanistan|invaded Afghanistan]] in October 2001 to depose the [[Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (1996–2001)|Taliban government]] in the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)|Afghan War]], which the U.S. suspected of protecting [[al-Qaeda]]. In December 2009, President [[Barack Obama]] ordered a "surge" in U.S. forces to Afghanistan, deploying an additional 30,000 troops to fight al-Qaeda and the [[Taliban insurgency]], before ordering a [[Withdrawal of United States troops from Afghanistan (2011–2016)|drawdown]] in 2011.<ref>{{cite news|work=CNN|url=https://www.cnn.com/2012/09/20/world/asia/afghanistan-us-troops/index.html|title=U.S. official: Afghanistan surge over as last of extra troops leave country|date=September 21, 2012|access-date=November 21, 2021}}</ref> Afghanistan continued to host U.S. and NATO [[Counterterrorism|counter-terror]] and counterinsurgency operations ([[International Security Assistance Force|ISAF]]/[[Resolute Support Mission|Resolute Support]] and operations [[Operation Enduring Freedom|Enduring Freedom]]/[[Operation Freedom's Sentinel|Freedom's Sentinel]]) until 2021, when the Taliban [[2021 Taliban offensive|retook control]] of Afghanistan amidst the [[Doha Agreement (2020)|negotiated]] [[2020–2021 U.S. troop withdrawal from Afghanistan|American-led withdrawal]] from the country. Over 2,400 Americans, 18 CIA operatives, and over 1,800 civilian contractors, [[United States military casualties in the War in Afghanistan|died]] in the Afghan War. The war in Afghanistan became the [[List of the lengths of United States participation in wars|longest war]] in United States history, lasting 19 years and ten months&ndash;surpassing the length of the Vietnam War, which lasted 19 years and five months–and cost the U.S. over $2 trillion.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2021/sep/21/richard-ojeda/did-us-spend-2-trillion-support-afghan-military/|title=Did the U.S. spend $2 trillion to support the Afghan military?|date=September 21, 2021|access-date=December 12, 2021|work=Politifact}}</ref>

Though "Operation Enduring Freedom" (OEF) usually refers to the 2001–2014 phase of the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–2021)|War in Afghanistan]], the term is also the U.S. military's official name for the war on terror, and has multiple subordinate operations which see American military forces deployed in regions across the world in the name of combating terrorism, often in collaboration with the host nation's central government via security cooperation and [[status of forces agreement]]s:
* [[Operation Enduring Freedom – Horn of Africa]] (OEF-HOA): U.S. forces deployed in [[Ethiopia]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/us-drone-base-in-ethiopia-is-operational/2011/10/27/gIQAznKwMM_story.html|newspaper=Washington Post|title=U.S. drone base in Ethiopia is operational|date=27 October 2011|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref> [[Kenya]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://allafrica.com/stories/202106140053.html|work=All Africa|title=Kenya: Biden to Send Troops to Kenya as U.S. Boosts War on Al-Shabaab|date=13 June 2021|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref> [[Liberia]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.africanews.com/2016/08/12/us-ends-six-year-military-mission-in-liberia//|work=Africa News|title=US ends six-year military mission in Liberia|date=8 December 2016|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref> [[Diego Garcia|Mauritius]], [[Rwanda]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://apanews.net/en/news/us-refutes-claims-of-establishing-a-military-base-in-rwanda|work=APA News|title=US refutes claims of establishing a military base in Rwanda|date=19 September 2020|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref> [[United States drone base in Seychelles|Seychelles]], [[Somalia]], skills|date=21 September 2011|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref> and [[Uganda]].<ref>{{cite training regional troops against Lord's Resistance Army|date=20 April 217|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/parallels/2018/04/28/605662771/the-military-doesnt-advertise-it-but-u-s-troops-are-all-over-africa|work=NPR|title=The Military Doesn't Advertise It, But U.S. **[[Camp Lemonnier]] is the only permanent U.S. military base in Africa, established in [[Djibouti]] in 2002, and supports OEF-HOA operations.
**The [[Peace Corps]] re-established a presence in [[Comoros]] in 2015, and [[Kentucky National Guard]] personnel have trained Comoros troops.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.state.gov/u-s-relations-with-comoros/|title=U.S. Relations With Comoros|date=3 December 2020|access-date=22 November 2021|work=United States Department of State}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nationalguard.mil/News/Article/574364/kentucky-soldiers-make-big-impact-on-small-comoros-islands/|title=Kentucky Soldiers make big impact on small Comoros islands|date=8 April 2013|access-date=22 November 2021|work=NationalGuard.mil}}</ref>

Niger|Niger]], [[Nigeria]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://onyxnewsng.com/2021/07/09/us-army-forces-nigerian-navy-special-boat-service-hold-joint-training/|title=US Army Forces, Nigerian Navy Special Boat Service Hold Joint Training|work=Oxy News Nigeria|date=9 July 2021|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref> [[Senegal]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-senegal-security/u-s-and-senegal-sign-defense-cooperation-deal-idUSKCN0XT1Q5|work=Reuters|title=U.S. and Senegal sign defense cooperation deal|date=2 May 2016|access-date=22 November 2021}}</ref> and [[Tunisia]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.africanews.com/2020/10/01/tunisia-signs-10-year-military-deal-with-us//|work=Africa News|date=10 January 2020|access-date=22 November 2021|title=Tunisia signs 10-year military deal with US}}</ref>
