**President Barack Obama deployed up to 300 U.S. troops to Cameroon in October 2015 to conduct [[Intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition, and reconnaissance#ISR (Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance)|intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance]] operations against the [[Boko Haram insurgency|Boko Haram]] terrorist group.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.aljazeera.com/news/2015/10/usa-troops-deployed-cameroon-boko-haram-fight-151014212428195.html |title=US troops deployed to Cameroon for Boko Haram fight |publisher=Al Jazeera English |date=14 October 2015 |access-date=25 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151018055734/http://www.aljazeera.com/news/2015/10/usa-troops-deployed-cameroon-boko-haram-fight-151014212428195.html |archive-date=18 October 2015 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Contingency Location Garoua]], a U.S. Army outpost housing around 200 troops and contractors in [[Garoua]], was established by 2017.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.army.mil/article/187679/isolated_from_us_military_small_army_post_looks_to_rid_terrorism_in_west_africa |publisher=[[Army News Service]] |first=Sean |last=Kimmons |date=November 27, 2017 |title=Isolated from US military, small Army post looks to rid terrorism in West Africa}}</ref>
**U.S. forces [[US military intervention in Niger|intervened in Niger in 2013]] to support French counter-terrorism efforts. In October 2017, four U.S. special operations soldiers and five Nigeriens were killed during an [[Islamic State – Sahil Province|Islamic State]] [[Tongo Tongo ambush|ambush]] in Niger in October 2017. There were around 800 U.S. military personnel in Niger at the time, most of whom were working on constructing a secondary drone base for U.S. and French aircraft in [[Agadez]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Schmitt|first1=Eric|last2=Gibbons-Neff|first2=Thomas|title=Deadly Ambush of Green Berets in Niger Belies a 'Low-Risk' Mission|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/05/world/africa/green-berets-killed-niger.html|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=20 October 2017|location=Washington|date=5 October 2017}}</ref> U.S. forces withdrew from Niger in 2024 at the request of the country's [[National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland|military junta]], losing access to [[Niger Air Base 201]], the largest drone base in Africa built by the U.S.<ref>{{cite news | title=Niger's Military Junta Ditches America and Courts Russia |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2024-03-19/next-africa-us-right-to-operate-drone-base-in-niger-terminated-by-junta |website=Bloomberg |date=March 19, 2024 |publisher=Bloomberg |access-date=May 2, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2024/09/16/politics/us-military-niger-withdrawal/index.html|work=CNN|date=16 September 2024|access-date=5 January 2025|title= US military completes withdrawal from Niger}}</ref>
**U.S. forces conducted [[2025 United States strikes in Nigeria|airstrikes]] against [[Islamic State – Sahel Province]] (ISSP) targets in Nigeria's [[Sokoto State]] on December 25, 2025, in coordination with the Nigerian government.<ref>{{cite web |author=Caleb Weiss |date=26 December 2025 |title=US strikes Islamic State in Nigeria |url=https://www.longwarjournal.org/archives/2025/12/us-strikes-islamic-state-in-nigeria.php |access-date=27 December 2025 |work=[[FDD's Long War Journal]]}}</ref> In February 2026, the U.S. deployed around 200 troops to the country to train Nigerian forces amid the [[Boko Haram insurgency]].<ref>{{cite news|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/us-military-says-some-forces-have-been-dispatched-nigeria-2026-02-03/|title=US military says some forces have been dispatched to Nigeria|date=February 3, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.militarytimes.com/news/pentagon-congress/2026/02/13/pentagon-to-deploy-roughly-200-troops-to-nigeria/|work=Military Times|title=Pentagon to deploy roughly 200 troops to Nigeria|date=13 February 2026|access-date=14 February 2026}}</ref>

Tucker]]|title=The Encyclopedia of Middle East Wars: The United States in the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan, and Iraq Conflicts [5 volumes]: The United States in the Persian Gulf, Afghanistan, and Iraq Conflicts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U05OvsOPeKMC&pg=PA415|date=8 October 2010|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-85109-948-1|page=415|access-date=17 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160101094429/https://books.google.com/books?id=U05OvsOPeKMC&pg=PA415|archive-date=1 January 2016|url-status=live}}<br />{{cite book|author1=Raymond Monsour Scurfield|author2=Katherine Theresa Platoni|title=War Trauma and Its Wake: Expanding the Circle of Healing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T--SxPDKjh4C&pg=PA268|date=10 September 2012|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-45788-3|page=268|access-date=17 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160611044449/https://books.google.com/books?id=T--SxPDKjh4C&pg=PA268|archive-date=11 June 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Flickr - The U.S. Army - 82nd Airborne re-enlistment ceremony.jpg|thumb|82nd Airborne at the [[Victory Arch]] in [[Baghdad]], Iraq, 2009. U.S. forces established the [[Green Zone]] in Baghdad during the 2003 invasion of Iraq.]]
In 2003, the U.S. and a [[Multi-National Force – Iraq|multi-national coalition]] [[2003 invasion of Iraq|invaded]] and [[Occupation of Iraq (2003–2011)|occupied]] Iraq to depose President [[Saddam Hussein]], whom the [[Presidency of George W. Bush|Bush administration]] [[Rationale for the Iraq War|accused]] of having [[Saddam Hussein and al-Qaeda link allegations|links]] to al-Qaeda and possessing [[Iraq and weapons of mass destruction|weapons of mass destruction]] (WMDs) during the [[Iraq disarmament crisis]]. No stockpiles of WMDs were discovered besides about 500 degraded and abandoned chemical munitions leftover from the [[Iran–Iraq War]] in the 1980s, which the [[Iraq Survey Group]] deemed "not militarily significant".<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/middle_east/3718150.stm |title=BBC NEWS {{pipe}} World {{pipe}} Middle East {{pipe}} Report concludes no WMD in Iraq |access-date=6 October 2004 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051102190832/http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/world/middle_east/3718150.stm |archive-date=2 November 2005 |url-status=live |df=dmy-all }}</ref> The U.S. [[United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence|Senate Select Committee on Intelligence]] found no substantial evidence of links between Iraq and al-Qaeda<ref>[http://intelligence.senate.gov/phaseiiaccuracy.pdf United States Senate Select Committee on Intelligence] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060921074629/http://intelligence.senate.gov/phaseiiaccuracy.pdf |date=2006-09-21 }} Retrieved September 10, 2006.</ref> and President Bush later admitted that "much of the intelligence turned out to be wrong".<ref>{{cite news |title=Bush takes responsibility for invasion intelligence |publisher=CNN |date=2005-12-14 |url=http://www.cnn.com/2005/POLITICS/12/14/bush.iraq/index.html |access-date=2006-02-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060211222322/http://www.cnn.com/2005/POLITICS/12/14/bush.iraq/index.html |archive-date=2006-02-11 |url-status=live }}</ref> Over 4,400 Americans and hundreds of thousands of Iraqi civilians [[Casualties of the Iraq War|died]] during the [[Iraq War]], which officially ended on December 18, 2011. The 2011 American withdrawal from Iraq was in accordance with the [[U.S.–Iraq Status of Forces Agreement]].

In the late 2000s, the [[United States Naval Forces Europe-Africa]] built the [[Africa Partnership Station]] to train coastal African nations in [[maritime security]], including enforcing laws in their territorial waters and [[exclusive economic zone]]s and combating piracy, smuggling, and [[illegal fishing]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.usni.org/2019/08/07/navy-says-africa-mission-more-about-building-partnerships-less-about-countering-china|title=Navy Says Africa Mission More About Building Partnerships, Less About Countering China|work=USNI News|date=7 August 2019|access-date=9 January 2022}}</ref> By 2009, the U.S. provided large amounts of aid and counterinsurgency training to enhance stability and reduce violence in President [[Álvaro Uribe]]'s war-ravaged Colombia, in what has been called "the most successful [[nation-building]] exercise by the United States in this century".<ref>{{cite journal|last=Boot|first=Max|author-link=Max Boot|author2=Richard Bennet|date=December 14, 2009|title=The Colombian Miracle|url=http://www.weeklystandard.com/Content/Public/Articles/000/000/017/301nyrut.asp?page=1|url-status=dead|journal=[[The Weekly Standard]]|volume=15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222024008/https://www.weeklystandard.com/Content/Public/Articles/000/000/017/301nyrut.asp?page=1|archive-date=22 February 2014|number=13}}</ref>

=== Arab Spring and Operation Inherent Resolve ===
{{Main|Arab Spring}}
{{See also|Operation Spartan Shield}}
[[File:Al-Tanf.jpg|thumb|left|A [[landing zone]] in [[al-Tanf]] during the [[U.S. intervention in the Syrian civil war]]]]

The 2011 [[Arab Spring]] resulted in uprisings, revolutions, and civil wars across the [[Arab world]], including [[Libyan civil war (2011)|Libya]], [[Syrian civil war|Syria]], and [[Yemeni civil war (2014–present)|Yemen]]. In 2011, the U.S. and [[NATO]] intervened in Libya by launching an [[2011 military intervention in Libya|extensive bombardment campaign]] in support of [[anti-Gaddafi forces]]. There was also speculation in ''[[The Washington Post]]'' that President [[Barack Obama]] issued a covert action, discovering in March 2011 that Obama authorized the CIA to carry out a clandestine effort to provide arms and support to the Libyan opposition.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/in-libya-cia-is-gathering-intelligence-on-rebels/2011/03/30/AFLyb25B_story.html |title=In Libya, CIA is gathering intelligence on rebels |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=March 30, 2011 |access-date=May 19, 2011 |first=Greg |last=Jaffe}}</ref> Libyan leader [[Muammar Gaddafi]] was ultimately overthrown and [[Killing of Muammar Gaddafi|killed]]. American activities in Libya resulted in the [[2012 Benghazi attack]]. 

Beginning around 2012, under the aegis of operation [[Timber Sycamore]] and [[Syrian Train and Equip Program|other clandestine activities]], [[CIA activities in Syria|CIA operatives]] and [[United States special operations forces|U.S. special operations troops]] trained and armed nearly 10,000 [[Syrian opposition|Syrian rebel fighters]] against Syrian president [[Bashar al-Assad]]<ref>{{cite news |title=U.S. has secretly provided arms training to Syria rebels from 2012 |url=https://www.latimes.com/nation/sns-la-fg-cia-syria-20130622-story.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130623024255/http://articles.latimes.com/2013/jun/21/world/la-fg-cia-syria-20130622 |url-status=live |archive-date=June 23, 2013 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=21 June 2013}}</ref> at a cost of $1 billion a year until it was phased out in 2017 by the Trump administration.<ref>{{cite news|title=Secret CIA effort in Syria faces large funding cut |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/lawmakers-move-to-curb-1-billion-cia-program-to-train-syrian-rebels/2015/06/12/b0f45a9e-1114-11e5-adec-e82f8395c032_story.html |newspaper=The Washington Post |date= 12 June 2015}}</ref><ref name="jaffe">{{cite news|last1=Jaffe|first1=Greg|last2=Entous|first2=Adam|title=Trump ends covert CIA program to arm anti-Assad rebels in Syria, a move sought by Moscow|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/national-security/trump-ends-covert-cia-program-to-arm-anti-assad-rebels-in-syria-a-move-sought-by-moscow/2017/07/19/b6821a62-6beb-11e7-96ab-5f38140b38cc_story.html|access-date=20 July 2017|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=19 July 2017}}</ref><ref name=wp-20170720>{{cite news|author-link=David Ignatius|last=Ignatius|first=David|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/what-the-demise-of-the-cias-anti-assad-program-means/2017/07/20/f6467240-6d87-11e7-b9e2-2056e768a7e5_story.html|title=What the demise of the CIA's anti-Assad program means|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=2017-07-20|access-date=2017-07-23}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Ali Watkins|title=Top general confirms end to secret U.S. program in Syria|url=https://www.politico.com/story/2017/07/21/tony-thomas-syria-secret-program-cia-240818|access-date=20 July 2017|work=Politico|date=21 July 2017}}</ref> After over a decade of civil war, Bashar al-Assad was ultimately [[Fall of the Assad regime|overthrown]] in December 2024 after a surprise [[2024 Syrian opposition offensives|rebel offensive]]. In December 2025, the US launched new [[Operation Hawkeye Strike|airstrikes]] after two US troops and an [[Interpreter officer|interpreter]] were killed in an [[December 2025 Palmyra attack|ambush]] near [[Palmyra (modern)|Palmyra]].

2013–2014 saw the [[Territory of the Islamic State|rise]] of the [[Islamic State|Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant]] (ISIL/ISIS) terror organization in the Middle East. In June 2014, during [[Operation Inherent Resolve]], the U.S. [[US-led intervention in Iraq (2014–2021)|re-intervened]] into Iraq and began [[International military intervention against ISIL#U.S. airstrikes|airstrikes]] against ISIL there in response to [[Iraqi Civil War (2014–2017)|prior gains]] by the terrorist group that threatened U.S. assets (including the [[Embassy of the United States, Baghdad|U.S. embassy]]) and Iraqi government forces. This was followed by more [[International military intervention against the Islamic State#Multi-national airstrikes|airstrikes]] on ISIL in Syria in September 2014,<ref name="hp1">{{cite news |author=Julian E. Barnes and Dion Nissenbaum |date=7 August 2014 |title=U.S., Arab Allies Launch Airstrikes Against Islamic State Targets in Syria |url=https://online.wsj.com/articles/us-arab-allies-launch-airstrikes-against-islamic-state-targets-in-syria-1411436642 |newspaper=[[Wall Street Journal]] |access-date=25 September 2014}}</ref> where the U.S.-led [[American-led intervention in the Syrian Civil War|coalition]] targeted ISIL positions throughout the country. Initial airstrikes involved fighters, bombers, and cruise missiles. The U.S. officially [[American intervention in Libya (2015–2019)|re-intervened]] in Libya in 2015 as part of Inherent Resolve.

In March 2015, President Obama declared that he had authorized U.S. forces to provide logistical and intelligence support to [[Saudi Arabia]] in their [[Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen|military intervention in Yemen]], establishing a "[[Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen#United States|Joint Planning Cell]]" with them.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/middle_east/report-yemens-embattled-president-flees-stronghold-as-rebels-advance/2015/03/25/e0913ae2-d2d5-11e4-a62f-ee745911a4ff_story.html |title=Saudi Arabia launches air attacks in Yemen| newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|date=25 March 2015}}</ref> American and British forces participated in the [[blockade of Yemen]]. In 2024, in response to [[Houthi movement|Houthi]] [[Houthi attacks on commercial vessels|attacks]] on commercial and naval vessels during the [[Red Sea crisis]], the UK and the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|Biden administration]] launched a [[US-led airstrike campaign in Yemen|new bombing campaign]] in Yemen, which was [[March 2025 United States attacks in Yemen|continued]] by the [[Foreign policy of the second Donald Trump administration|Donald Trump administration]] before arranging a bilateral [[2025 United States–Houthi ceasefire|ceasefire]].<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Schmitt |first1=Eric |last2=Swan |first2=Jonathan |date=2025-03-15 |title=U.S. Launches Broad Attack on Militant Sites in Yemen |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/15/us/politics/us-attack-houthis.html |access-date=2025-03-15 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US }}</ref>

By 2017 the [[MV Ocean Trader|MV ''Ocean Trader'']], a discreet Special Warfare Support vessel operated by [[Military Sealift Command]], was in operation. The ''Ocean Trader'' serves as a floating, mobile barracks and command center for [[United States special operations forces|U.S. special operations units]] abroad. The "mothership" increases their deployability range when called upon for missions and foreign interventions.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://taskandpurpose.com/news/mv-ocean-trader-caribbean/|work=Task and Purpose|title=The elusive ship built to carry US special operators is in the Caribbean|date=25 September 2025|access-date=11 January 2026}}</ref>

In March 2021, the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|Biden administration]] designated [[Al-Shabaab (Mozambique)|al-Shabaab in Mozambique]] as a terrorist organization and, at the request of the [[Mozambique]] government, intervened in the [[Insurgency in Cabo Delgado|Cabo Delgado conflict]]. [[United States Army Special Forces|Army Special Forces]] were deployed in the country to train Mozambican marines.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.state.gov/state-department-terrorist-designations-of-isis-affiliates-and-leaders-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-and-mozambique/|work=United States Department of State|date=10 March 2021|access-date=21 November 2021|title=State Department Terrorist Designations of ISIS Affiliates and Leaders in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mozambique}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-56441499|title=Mozambique conflict: Why are US forces there?|work=BBC News |date=Mar 21, 2021|access-date=Mar 22, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/green-berets-to-battle-isis-insurgents-accused-of-beheading-children-2021-3|title=US deploys Green Berets to defeat ISIS-linked insurgents accused of beheading children on a new front in southern Africa|date=Mar 20, 2021|access-date=Mar 22, 2021|via=[www.businessinsider.com}}](https://www.businessinsider.com}})</ref>

During his [[First presidency of Donald Trump|first term]], President [[Donald Trump]] was the first U.S. president in decades to [[Foreign policy of the first Donald Trump administration#Overseas presence|not commit the military to new foreign campaigns]], instead continuing wars and operations he inherited from his predecessors, including interventions in Iraq, Syria and Somalia.<ref>{{cite news|title=Love Him Or Hate Him, President Trump's Defense Legacy Is Profound|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/lorenthompson/2020/12/15/love-him-or-hate-him-president-trumps-defense-legacy-is-profound/|work=Forbes|date=15 December 2020|access-date=9 January 2022}}</ref> The Trump administration often used economic pressure against international adversaries such as [[Venezuela]] and the [[Iran|Islamic Republic of Iran]].<ref>[https://www.wsj.com/articles/trump-wields-u-s-economic-might-in-struggles-with-allies-and-adversaries-alike-11579280987 "Trump Wields U.S. Economic Might in Struggles With Allies and Adversaries Alike"], ''Wall Street Journal'', Jan. f17, 2020</ref> In 2019, tensions between the U.S. and Iran triggered a crisis in the Persian Gulf which saw the U.S. bolster its military presence in the region, the creation of the [[International Maritime Security Construct]] to combat attacks on commercial shipping, and the [[Assassination of Qasem Soleimani|assassination]] of prominent Iranian general [[Qasem Soleimani]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2020/01/03/qasem-soleimani-killing-us-send-more-soldiers-middle-east/2805493001/|title=US to send 3,000 more soldiers to the Middle East in the wake of Qasem Soleimani killing|last1=Wu|first1=Nicholas|date=3 January 2020|work=USA Today|access-date=3 January 2020|url-status=live|last2=Brook|first2=Tom Vanden|department=World|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200103193328/https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/world/2020/01/03/qasem-soleimani-killing-us-send-more-soldiers-middle-east/2805493001/|archive-date=3 January 2020}}</ref>

== Trump Corollary ==
{{Further|Donroe Doctrine|American expansionism under Donald Trump}}
[[File:United States Foreign Interventions in 2025.png|thumb|Foreign interventions by the United States during 2025]]
The [[Foreign policy of the second Trump administration|second Trump administration]] introduced the [[Donroe Doctrine|Trump Corollary]] to the [[Monroe Doctrine#America First and Trump Corollary|Monroe Doctrine]], which aimed to "reassert and enforce the Monroe Doctrine to restore American [[America's Backyard|pre-eminence]] in the Western Hemisphere."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/world/americas/trumps-donroe-doctrine-aims-to-dominate-the-americas-b31208dd?gaa_at=eafs&gaa_n=AWEtsqdPSoehJ-K3oogmJSiDR-7D6LmZLI5D5TZX8H6zlMnz8EyuQvRJdRf3gWjPzNk%3D&gaa_ts=693bcb37&gaa_sig=hah-XwLmB0GEiTRfwom148gaijHWJBGYHLTsX8UpwWKN1Wv-ZadnVcy3sjlkZWaMv8fROBJg1Kuk7JW8qF3TAQ%3D%3D|work=The Wall Street Journal|title=Trump's 'Donroe Doctrine' Aims to Dominate the Americas|date=October 22, 2025|access-date=December 12, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|work=New York Times|title=The 'Donroe Doctrine': Trump's Bid to Control the Western Hemisphere|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/17/world/americas/trump-latin-america-monroe-doctrine.html|date=November 17, 2025|access-date=December 12, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.economist.com/the-americas/2025/12/10/how-the-donroe-doctrine-is-changing-puerto-rico|newspaper=The Economist|date=December 10, 2025|access-date=December 12, 2025|title=How the "Donroe Doctrine" is changing Puerto Rico}}</ref> President Trump embraced an [[American expansionism under Donald Trump|expansionist policy]] in the Western Hemisphere, openly threatening to annex [[Movements for the annexation of Canada to the United States#Proposals to annex Canada by President Donald Trump|Canada]], [[Greenland crisis|Greenland]], and the [[History of the Panama Canal#Demands by Donald Trump to reclaim U.S. control of the canal|Panama Canal]]. In December 2025 the U.S. Army established the [[United States Army Western Hemisphere Command|Western Hemisphere Command]], uniting [[FORSCOM]], [[United States Army North|ARNORTH]] and [[United States Army South|ARSOUTH]] under a unified headquarters overseeing operations across North America, Latin America, and the Caribbean.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-12-05 |title=US Army activates Western Hemisphere Command in historic transition ceremony |url=https://www.army.mil/article/289410/us_army_activates_western_hemisphere_command_in_historic_transition_ceremony |access-date=2025-12-10 |website=[www.army.mil](https://www.army.mil) |language=en}}</ref>

The [[National Security Strategy (United States)#President Donald Trump, second term|2025 National Security Strategy]] (NSS) and the [[National Defense Strategy|2026 National Defense Strategy]] generally renounced America's prior role in [[Global policeman|world policing]] and reoriented towards transactional alliances, regionalism and [[Polarity (international relations)|multipolar]] [[spheres of influence]]. The NSS maintained goals of containing Chinese adventurism and militarily reinforcing the [[Island chain strategy|First Island Chain]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Troianovski|first=Anton|date=December 6, 2025|title=Trump's Security Strategy Focuses on Profit, Not Spreading Democracy|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/12/05/us/politics/trump-national-security-strategy.html|url-access=subscription|access-date=December 6, 2025}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2025-12-05 |title=Lots of pressure on allies, no mention of North Korea in White House national security strategy document |url=https://koreajoongangdaily.joins.com/news/2025-12-05/national/defense/Lots-of-pressure-on-allies-no-mention-of-North-Korea-in-White-House-national-security-strategy-document/2471042 |access-date=2025-12-05 |website=koreajoongangdaily.joins.com |language=en}}</ref> The Trump administration played a role in mediating the [[2025 India–Pakistan conflict]]<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwyx5yw8y28o|work=BBC|title=Pakistan to nominate Trump for Nobel Peace Prize|date=21 June 2025|access-date=22 June 2025}}</ref> alongside brokering and facilitating peace agreements between the [[2025 Democratic Republic of the Congo–Rwanda peace agreement|DR Congo and Rwanda]], [[Armenia–Azerbaijan peace agreement|Armenia and Azerbaijan]], and [[Kuala Lumpur Peace Accord|Cambodia and Thailand]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c93dy2kk7vzo|work=BBC|date=26 October 2025|title=Trump presides over Thai-Cambodia 'peace deal' - but what does it mean?}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/2025/08/20/donald-trump-six-wars/85721555007/|work=USA Today |title=What six wars did Donald Trump end? See the list of conflicts he claims as settled|date=20 August 2025|access-date=27 August 2025}}</ref> The [[Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity]] was proposed along the [[Zangezur corridor]], linking Azerbaijan to [[Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic|Nakhchivan]] in Armenia.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/abc123xyz|title=Armenia's pivot to West with 'Trump Corridor' deal sidelines Russia|newspaper=Financial Times|date=August 8, 2025|access-date=August 9, 2025}}</ref>

=== Latin America interventions ===
Trump intervened militarily, politically and economically in Latin America. In October 2025, he threatened to [[2025 United States–Argentina currency swap|cut off financial aid to Argentina]] if incumbent president [[Javier Milei]]'s party, [[La Libertad Avanza]], lost the [[2025 Argentine legislative election]], an election the party would go on to win decisively.<ref>{{cite news |title=Trump threatens to cut US aid to Argentina if Milei loses election |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/14/trump-threatens-to-cut-us-aid-to-argentina-if-milei-loses-election}}</ref> Trump attempted to influence the [[2025 Honduran general election]] by publicly supporting [[Nasry Asfura]] of the [[National Party of Honduras|National Party]] and warned that US aid could be suspended if Asfura did not win; Asfura was declared the victor a month later.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Trump says will pardon former Honduras leader before presidential vote|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/28/trump-says-will-pardon-former-honduras-leader-before-presidential-vote|website=Al Jazeera|access-date=|language=en|first=Joseph|last=Stepansky}}</ref> Trump's [[Immigration policy of the second Trump administration|immigration policy]] overlapped with foreign policy, with [[Nayib Bukele]]'s [[El Salvador]]<ref>{{cite web|last1=Roston|first1=Aram|last2=Hesson|first2=Ted|last3=Sequera|first3=Vivian|last4=Symmes Cobb|first4=Julia|last5=Cooke|first5=Kristina|last6=Kinosian|first6=Sarah|editor1-last=Durfee|editor1-first=Don|editor2-last=Nickel|editor2-first=Rod|editor3-last=O'Brien|editor3-first=Rosalba|date=18 July 2025|location=[[Washington, D.C.]] and [[Caracas]]|title=El Salvador Sends Detained Venezuelans Home in Swap for Americans|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/el-salvador-send-detained-venezuelans-home-swap-americans-sources-say-2025-07-18/|language=en|work=[[Reuters]]|access-date=18 July 2025}}</ref> and [[Luis Abinader]]'s [[Dominican Republic]]<ref>{{cite news|work=New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/12/world/americas/dominican-republic-deportees-us.html|title=Dominican Republic Agrees to Take Third-Country Migrants Deported by U.S.|date=12 May 2026|access-date=13 May 2026}}</ref> [[March 2025 American deportations of Venezuelans|cooperating]] with the U.S. in receiving [[Third country national|third country]] deportees in their respective countries. Trump reportedly desired [[2026 Cuban crisis|regime change in Cuba]], tightening the fuel blockade and further isolating the country.

The Trump administration also revamped the [[war on drugs]] by cracking down on [[Maritime drug trafficking in Latin America|drug trafficking]] in [[Latin America]] and [[:s:Executive Order 14157|designating]] [[Mexican drug war#Mexican cartels|Mexican]] and South American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/8/14/trump-administration-sanctions-two-mexican-drug-cartels-announces-bounties|title=Trump administration sanctions two Mexican drug cartels, announces bounties|date=14 August 2025|access-date=20 August 2005|work=Al Jazeera}}</ref> including Colombia's [[Clan del Golfo]] and Venezuela's [[Cartel of the Suns]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/us-designates-colombia-cartel-terrorist-group-clan-del-golfo/|work=CBS|title=U.S. designates notorious Colombian cartel a terrorist group, opening door to possible military action|date=December 17, 2025|access-date=December 18, 2025}}</ref> The [[Shield of the Americas]] coalition was established, allowing participating governments to coordinate anti-cartel efforts. The [[U.S. Coast Guard]] launched Operation Pacific Viper to combat drug trafficking in the eastern Pacific Ocean,<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/coast-guard-cocaine-seizure-operation-pacific-viper-shots-fired-video/|work=CBS News|title=Coast Guard releases video of cocaine seizure in Pacific, showing shots fired at alleged drug boat|date=December 10, 2025|access-date=December 13, 2025}}</ref> while [[Operation Southern Spear]], a separate [[United States military buildup in the Caribbean during Operation Southern Spear|military campaign]] prioritizing the Caribbean Sea, reactivated the [[Roosevelt Roads Naval Station]] in [[Ceiba, Puerto Rico]]. The US conducted [[United States strikes on alleged drug traffickers during Operation Southern Spear|airstrikes]] on alleged drug smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, reportedly supported by intelligence provided by the CIA.<ref name=boats>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2025/08/15/politics/us-military-deploying-caribbean-latin-america-cartel-mission|work=CNN|title=US military deploying over 4,000 additional troops to waters around Latin America as part of Trump's counter-cartel mission|date=15 August 2025|access-date=20 August 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/21/us-strikes-caribbean-cia-role |last=Roston |first=Aram |title=CIA playing 'most important part' in US strikes in the Caribbean, sources say |work=The Guardian |date=21 October 2025 |access-date=21 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251021113929/https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/21/us-strikes-caribbean-cia-role |archive-date=21 October 2025|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/munition-sept-2-boat-strike-intended-kill-people/story?id=128352628|work=ABC News|title=Munition used in Sept. 2 boat strike was intended to kill people, top Democrat says|date=December 12, 2025|access-date=December 13, 2025}}</ref> The CIA reportedly escalated lethal covert operations (including [[car bomb]]ings) inside Mexico to weaken the cartels, though the CIA publicly denied these reports.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2026/05/12/politics/cia-drug-cartels-deadly-operations-mexico|work=CNN|title=Exclusive: CIA escalates secret war on cartels with deadly operations inside Mexico|date=12 May 2026|access-date=4 August 2026}}</ref>

In March 2026 the U.S. and [[Ecuador]] launched [[Ecuadorian conflict (2024–present)|joint operations]] against "narco-terrorist" groups, including [[:es:Comandos de la Frontera|Comandos de la Frontera]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.faz.net/aktuell/politik/usa-unter-trump/operation-southern-spear-us-armee-bekaempft-drogenbanden-jetzt-auch-in-ecuador-110847521.html|title=„Operation Southern Spear“: US-Armee bekämpft Drogenbanden jetzt auch in Ecuador|date=4 March 2026|website=Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung|accessdate=7 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.com/International/us-military-carries-1st-land-operation-cartels-ecuador/story?id=130739672|work=ABC News|title=US military assists Ecuador in 1st land operation against cartels: Source|date=3 March 2026|access-date=7 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/us-conducts-lethal-operations-ecuador-military-says-2026-03-06/|work=Reuters|title=US, Ecuador bomb drug trafficker camp near Colombia border, militaries say|date=6 March 2026|access-date=7 March 2026}}</ref> [[Guatemala]] requested U.S. military cooperation encompassing equipment, training, and experts to fight drug trafficking, but denied that it had authorized new U.S. military operations inside the country.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/guatemala-agrees-joint-strikes-with-us-against-drug-gangs-nyt-reports-2026-05-28/|title=Guatemala outlines deal for US aid against drug trafficking|work=Reuters|date=28 May 2026|access-date=4 August 2026}}</ref>

=== 2025–2026 Iran conflict ===
{{Expand section|date=March 2026}}
{{Main|2026 Iran war|2026 United States naval blockade of Iran|Operation Project Freedom}}
Trump inherited a [[Middle Eastern crisis (2023–present)|crisis in the Middle East]] and the ongoing [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]]. On June 22, 2025,Trump carried out airstrikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, coordinating with Israel amid the twelve-day Iran–Israel war. The strikes temporarily disrupted Iran’s nuclear activities and drew international attention, with the UN expressing alarm and calling for restraint.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Drummond |first=Michael |last2=Reporter |first2=Foreign News |last3=Carroll |first3=Mickey |last4=reporter |title=US warplanes strike three nuclear sites as Iran warns of 'everlasting' consequences |url=https://news.sky.com/story/fordow-is-gone-us-warplanes-strike-three-nuclear-sites-in-iran-13386910 |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=Sky News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-06-22 |title=Alarm grows after the US inserts itself into Israel's war against Iran with strikes on nuclear sites |url=https://apnews.com/article/israel-iran-war-nuclear-trump-bomber-news-06-22-2025-c2baca52babe915e033ae175ce8b2687 |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lawal |first=Shola |title=How does US military build-up off Iran compare to the June 2025 strikes? |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/29/how-does-us-military-build-up-off-iran-compare-to-the-june-2025-strikes |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref> These strikes were carried out for the "defense of its Israeli ally",<ref>{{Cite web |title=Operation Epic Fury and International Law |url=https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-legal-adviser/2026/04/operation-epic-fury-and-international-law/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=United States Department of State |language=en-US}}</ref> though the actual feasibility of the Iranian state acquiring a nuclear bomb capable of being a threat to Israel was contested.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vergano |first=Dan |title=Iran was nowhere close to a nuclear bomb, experts say |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/iran-was-nowhere-close-to-a-nuclear-bomb-experts-say/ |access-date=2026-05-27 |website=Scientific American |language=en}}</ref> Furthermore, the US-Israeli-Iranian conflict which proceeded has been viewed as widely ineffective and unpopular, costing american taxpayers 2 billion a day to operate. On September 29, 2025, he unveiled a 20-point [[Gaza peace plan|peace plan]] to resolve the [[Gaza War]], parts of which called for an [[International Stabilization Force]] and [[Board of Peace]].

== European Deterrence Initiative and Russo-Ukrainian War ==
In response to the 2014 [[Annexation of Crimea by the Russian Federation|Russian annexation of Crimea]], the Obama administration established the [[European Deterrence Initiative]] (EDI), a program dedicated to bolstering American military presence in [[Central and Eastern Europe]]. The EDI has funded [[Operation Atlantic Resolve]], a [[collective defense]] effort to enhance NATO's military planning and defense capabilities by maintaining a persistent rotation of American air, ground and naval presence in the region to deter perceived Russian aggression along NATO's eastern flank.<ref>[https://www.csis.org/analysis/european-reassurance-initiative-0 "FACT SHEET: European Reassurance Initiative and Other U.S. Efforts in Support of NATO Allies and Partners"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110092512/https://www.csis.org/analysis/european-reassurance-initiative-0|date=2017-01-10}}, Mark Cancian. Center for Strategic and International Studies. February 9, 2016. Retrieved January 9, 2017.</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=U.S. European Command|title=OPERATION ATLANTIC RESOLVE|url=http://www.defense.gov/home/features/2014/0514_atlanticresolve/FactSheet_OperationAtlanticResolve_3Jul14.pdf|website=United States Department of Defense|access-date=21 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150505190548/http://www.defense.gov/home/features/2014/0514_atlanticresolve/FactSheet_OperationAtlanticResolve_3Jul14.pdf|archive-date=2015-05-05|url-status=dead}}</ref> The [[NATO Enhanced Forward Presence|Enhanced Forward Presence]] (EFP) force was established by NATO.

=== Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative ===
{{Main|Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative}}

In early November 2024, the Biden administration lifted a ''de facto'' ban on U.S. military contractors deploying to Ukraine to help the [[Ukrainian military]] repair and maintain [[List of military aid to Ukraine during the Russo-Ukrainian War|U.S.-supplied weapons systems]] that require "specific technical expertise", such as [[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon#Ukraine|F-16 fighter jets]] and [[MIM-104 Patriot#Patriot operations in the Russo-Ukrainian War|Patriot air defense systems]]. Although various American companies already had personnel in Ukraine fulfilling contracts for the Ukrainian government, this new policy allowed the Pentagon to provide contracts to American companies for work inside Ukraine for the first time since [[Russian invasion of Ukraine|Russia invaded in 2022]]. Pentagon officials emphasized the contractors will be located far from the front lines and will not engage Russian forces, and the policy change will result in a range of a few dozen to a few hundred contractors working inside Ukraine at a time.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/11/08/politics/biden-administration-american-military-contractors-deploy-ukraine/index.html|work=CNN|date=8 November 2024|access-date=14 November 2024|title=Biden administration to allow American military contractors to deploy to Ukraine for first time since Russia's invasion}}</ref> On 17 November 2024, Biden allowed Ukraine to launch U.S.-made long-range missiles [[Use of long-range weapons by Ukraine in Russia|deep into Russian territory]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/biden-lifts-ban-ukraine-using-us-arms-strike-inside-russia-2024-11-17/|work=Reuters|date=17 November 2024|title=Biden allows Ukraine to use US arms to strike inside Russia}}</ref>

=== Lettergate ===
{{Main|Lettergate|Anti-Americanism in Pakistan}}

It is alleged that the United States was involved in the [[No-confidence motion against Imran Khan|2022 vote of no confidence]] against former Pakistani Prime Minister [[Imran Khan]]. On 7 March 2022, Islamabad's then-ambassador to the U.S., Asad Majeed Khan met with two American officials, one of whom was [[Donald Lu]], a United States diplomat serving as Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asian Affairs. In the meeting, Lu showed displeasure over Khan's visit to Russia one day before Russia's invasion of Ukraine.<ref name="Syed">{{Cite web |last=Syed |first=Baqir Sajjad |date=2022-04-08 |title='Cablegate' lands foreign service in knotty predicament |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1683975 |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=DAWN.COM |language=en}}</ref> He stated that if the no-confidence vote were to be successful, "all would be forgiven", otherwise ".. it will be tough going ahead".<ref name="Syed"/><ref>{{Cite news |last=Baloch |first=Shah Meer |date=2022-03-31 |title=Imran Khan claims US threatened him and wants him ousted as Pakistan PM |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/mar/31/imran-khan-address-pakistan-faces-no-confidence-vote |access-date=2023-08-10 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Threatening letter came from US: PM Imran Khan |url=https://www.thenews.com.pk/print/946252-threatening-letter-came-from-us-pm |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=[www.thenews.com.pk](https://www.thenews.com.pk) |date=April 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title='One-million gathering to be referendum against opposition' |url=https://www.thenews.com.pk/print/941544-one-million-gathering-to-be-referendum-against-opposition |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=[www.thenews.com.pk](https://www.thenews.com.pk) |date=March 15, 2022 |language=en}}</ref> It was only the next day, on 8 March 2022, that the [[Pakistan Democratic Movement]] announced that they were bringing a no-confidence motion against the then Premier. A cipher was sent to Khan with the details of the conversation between the officials. On 27 March 2022, Khan claimed that he possessed [[Lettergate|a diplomatic cable]] dated 7 March, in which a "threat" was issued by the US government stating their desire to see Khan's ousting from office, with the stipulation that Pakistan would be "forgiven" if the motion against him succeeded. The US was allegedly unhappy with Khan's foreign policy and his visit to Russia.<ref>{{cite news |title=Threat letter from US, says Pak PM Imran Khan says in slip of tongue |url=https://www.business-standard.com/article/international/threat-letter-from-us-says-pak-pm-imran-khan-says-in-slip-of-tongue-122033101557_1.html |work=Business Standard |agency=Press Trust of India |date=31 March 2022 }}</ref>

In August 2023, more than a year after Khan first made his claims, ''[[The Intercept]]'' published a leaked copy of the cable, which it claimed to have received from a disgruntled member of Pakistan's military. In the cable, Pakistan's ambassador to the United States reported that U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Central and South Asia [[Donald Lu]] warned that the "isolation of the Prime Minister will become very strong from Europe and the United States" after Khan's visit to Russia, and that "if the no-confidence vote against the Prime Minister succeeds, all will be forgiven in Washington."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hussain |first=Ryan Grim, Murtaza |date=2023-08-09 |title=Secret Pakistan Cable Documents U.S. Pressure to Remove Imran Khan |url=https://theintercept.com/2023/08/09/imran-khan-pakistan-cypher-ukraine-russia/ |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=The Intercept |language=en-US}}</ref>

Khan alleged that the United States was behind a "foreign conspiracy" to oust him in a [[United States involvement in regime change|regime change]], and that he had written evidence attesting to this. These allegations were denied by the US government. Imran Khan also said that he has been punished on not accepting U.S. policy after withdrawal from Afghanistan. Donald Lu evaded the question regarding his meeting with Pakistan's Ambassador to the U.S.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-04-05 |title=Lu evades question about Imran's allegations |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1683520 |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=DAWN.COM |language=en}}</ref> Khan's party alleged that there is a close connection between regime changes after UN's Ukraine Resolution. Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs Spokesperson [[Maria Zakharova]] said that the U.S. has punished disobedient Imran Khan and termed that interference a shameless act. However, the U.S. claims that there is "absolutely no truth" in the allegations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=US welcomes NSC statement |url=https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/952645-us-welcomes-nsc-statement-says-theres-absolutely-no-truth-to-conspiracy-allegations |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=[www.thenews.com.pk](https://www.thenews.com.pk) |date=April 23, 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Dawn.com |date=2020-11-11 |title=US embassy in Islamabad apologises for sharing 'unauthorised' tweet against PM Imran |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1589820 |access-date=2023-08-10 |website=DAWN.COM |language=en}}</ref>
